Halal, haram, droits, devoirs : ce que l’on ne dit pas du mariage en islam
items.description: CONTRIBUTION . Divorces précoces, couples en crise, imams débordés : et si notre discours sur le mariage en islam avait oublié l’essentiel ? À peine mariés, ils divorcent. Le nombre de divorces a explosé parmi les couples musulmans en France. Hausse des divorces parmi les couples musulmans en France : les imams en première ligne Dans les mosquées, les imams sont de plus en plus souvent appelés à régler des conflits conjugaux pour lesquels ils ne sont pas formés. Au lieu de contribuer à apaiser les tensions et à resserrer les liens du couple, ils peuvent parfois, malgré eux, les aggraver, en tenant un discours très technique, presque exclusivement centré sur le licite et l’illicite. Cela témoigne d’une connaissance encore insuffisante des dimensions éthiques, humaines et spirituelles du mariage en islam. Comme si connaître les règles du mariage suffisait à savoir vivre à deux. Une très grande partie de la littérature musulmane consacrée au mariage est centrée sur les droits et les devoirs. On y trouve beaucoup de règles, d’obligations, d’interdits… mais étonnamment peu de choses sur l’amour, la tendresse, la complicité, la paix intérieure, la miséricorde, l’écoute et l’harmonie conjugale. Pourtant, lorsque le Coran évoque le mariage, son vocabulaire est profondément spirituel et humain : « Parmi Ses signes, Il a créé pour vous, de vous-mêmes, des épouses auprès desquelles vous trouvez la tranquillité, et Il a établi entre vous affection et miséricorde ». (Coran, 30:21) Sakîna (apaisement), mawadda (affection) et rahma (miséricorde) : voilà les notions qui devraient être au cœur de notre réflexion sur le mariage. Un discours trop centré sur le contrat Que transmettons-nous trop souvent aux jeunes musulmans lorsqu’ils se préparent au mariage ? Une longue liste de droits et de devoirs, comme si le mariage était avant tout un contrat juridique à gérer, plutôt qu’une relation humaine et spirituelle à construire. J’ai longtemps pensé que cette approche concernait principalement les sociétés musulmanes traditionnelles, notamment dans les pays arabes. Je constate aujourd’hui, avec une certaine tristesse, qu’elle est également très présente en Europe, et plus particulièrement en France. Le plus préoccupant, dans tout cela, c’est que les institutions musulmanes, et plus particulièrement les imams, tombent eux aussi, parfois en première ligne, dans ce piège. En reproduisant inlassablement un discours centré presque exclusivement sur les droits et les devoirs, ils risquent d’enfermer les jeunes dans une vision du mariage réduite à une logique juridique et normative, et de les détourner de sa dimension humaine, affective et spirituelle . Le droit ne suffit pas à faire un foyer Il ne s’agit évidemment pas d’opposer le droit à l’amour, ni de nier l’importance des droits et des devoirs. Mais un mariage ne se construit pas uniquement avec des règles juridiques. On peut connaître parfaitement les droits de son conjoint et être incapable de lui donner de la tendresse. On peut connaître tous ses devoirs et ne jamais savoir écouter. On peut savoir ce qui est halal et haram et pourtant rendre son conjoint profondément malheureux. La question n’est donc pas seulement : « Quels sont mes droits et quels sont tes devoirs ? » La question devrait aussi être : Est-ce que je suis pour toi une source de tranquillité ? Est-ce que tu te sens aimé(e) auprès de moi ? Est-ce que je suis un refuge pour toi, comme tu peux l’être pour moi ? Est-ce que notre foyer est un lieu de miséricorde ? Car le mariage n’est pas seulement un statut juridique. C’est une relation qui se construit chaque jour, par les paroles, les gestes, l’écoute, le pardon, la bienveillance et la capacité à prendre soin de l’autre. Former des imams capables d’accompagner les couples Il est peut-être temps de rééquilibrer profondément notre discours sur le mariage. Le mariage en islam n’est pas seulement une affaire de halal et de haram. C’est aussi une affaire de sakîna , de mawadda et de rahma : de tranquillité, d’affection et de miséricorde, comme nous le rappelle si justement le Coran. Les parents doivent prendre conscience de la façon dont ils transmettent ces valeurs à leurs enfants. Quant aux imams, il est urgent que leur formation intègre pleinement ces dimensions du mariage, ainsi que des éléments de psychologie, de thérapie conjugale et de vie de couple. Car un imam peut parfaitement maîtriser les règles du mariage et être démuni face à un couple qui ne communique plus, à une épouse qui ne se sent plus aimée, à un mari qui ne sait plus comment dialoguer avec sa femme, ou à deux personnes qui ont perdu toute confiance l’une envers l’autre. Il ne s’agit pas de transformer l’imam en psychologue ou en thérapeute. Il s’agit de lui donner les outils nécessaires pour écouter, comprendre ses limites, accompagner avec discernement et orienter, lorsque cela est nécessaire, vers des professionnels compétents. Nos enfants ne nous demanderont pas si nous connaissions par cœur les droits et les devoirs du mariage. Ils nous demanderont si, à la maison, ils ont vu de la tendresse, entendu des mots doux, et senti que notre foyer était un lieu de paix, d’affection et de miséricorde. *Azzedine Gaci est le recteur de la mosquée de Villeurbanne Important : Les tribunes publiées sur TSA ont pour but de permettre aux lecteurs de participer au débat. Elles ne reflètent pas la position de la rédaction de notre média. L’article Halal, haram, droits, devoirs : ce que l’on ne dit pas du mariage en islam est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Nigeria leads Africa investability gains
items.description: •Up four places in Bloomberg’s ranking By Yinka Kolawole Nigeria has emerged as the biggest climber among major African economies in Bloomberg Economics’ 2026 Investment Risk-O-Meter, rising four places to eighth position on the back of improved economic and fiscal fundamentals. The latest scorecard released yesterday, which assesses the relative investability of 19 African economies, ranked Mauritius first, while Nigeria overtook Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya and Namibia to secure the eighth position. Bloomberg said Nigeria’s improved ranking reflected gains in three of the five metrics assessed by the gauge – economic strength, fiscal strength and external vulnerability. “The continent’s biggest oil producer and refiner rose four places to eighth in the 2026 Bloomberg Economics Investment Risk-O-Meter, overtaking Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya and Namibia as it improved in three of the five metrics assessed by the gauge – economic strength, fiscal strength and external vulnerability,” Bloomberg said. The development comes amid ongoing economic reforms by the Federal Government aimed at tackling longstanding fiscal, foreign exchange and power-sector challenges. Nigeria’s improved standing follows a series of policy changes introduced since President Bola Tinubu assumed office in 2023, including the removal of the petrol subsidy, liberalisation of the foreign exchange market and the introduction of electricity tariffs aimed at reducing losses in the power sector. The reforms, though initially accompanied by higher costs and significant pressure on businesses and households, have increasingly been viewed by investors as measures aimed at restoring macroeconomic stability and improving the operating environment. Nigeria’s gain contrasts with weaker performances by some other major African economies. Botswana fell two places, while South Africa, which topped the ranking last year, dropped one spot, partly due to weaker economic-growth outlooks. Mauritius now ranks first for relative investability among the 19 economies assessed, underscoring its continued strength across key investment-risk indicators. Nigeria’s latest ranking marks a significant improvement in its relative investment position on the continent and could strengthen investor confidence if the reform momentum is sustained and translated into stronger growth, improved fiscal outcomes and greater macroeconomic stability. items.title: Capital importation rises 102% to $16.4bn in 5mths
items.description: By Babajide Komolafe Capital importation into the country rose by 101.8 per cent, year-on-year, YoY to $16.41 billion in the five months to May 2026 from $8.13 billion in the same period of 2025. Vanguard analysis of the monthly economic reports of the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, from January to May 2026, showed that the growth in capital importation was driven by Foreign Portfolio Investment, FPI, which rose by 114.42 per cent, YoY to $15.61 billion in 5M’26 from $7.28 billion in 5M’25. Consequently, FPI’s share of total capital importation expanded further to 95.12 per cent in 5M’26 from 89.54 per cent in 5M’25. However, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and Other Investments recorded marginal declines of 9.5 per cent and 7.69 per cent, YoY, respectively, in 5M ‘26. FDI dropped to $0.19 billion in 5M’26 from $0.21 billion in 5M’25. Similarly, Other Investments — comprising foreign loans and trade credits — fell to $0.60 billion in 5M’26 from $0.65 billion in 5M’25. On a month-on-month, MoM, basis, total capital importation declined by 14.8 per cent to $3.0 billion in February from $3.52 billion in January. It, however, rebounded strongly by 28.3 per cent to $3.85 billion in March, before declining by 26.8 per cent to $2.82 billion in April. Capital importation recovered again in May, rising by 14.2 per cent to $3.22 billion. The monthly trend showed that the volatility in total capital importation was largely driven by movements in FPI, which accounted for more than 90 per cent of total inflows in each of the five months. FPI declined by 14.8 per cent MoM to $2.87 billion in February from $3.37 billion in January. It subsequently surged by 26.1 per cent to $3.62 billion in March, before falling by 26.5 per cent to $2.66 billion in April. In May, FPI rebounded by 16.2 per cent to $3.09 billion. FDI rose by 33.3 per cent MoM to $0.04 billion in February from $0.03 billion in January and increased further by 50 per cent to $0.06 billion in March. It then fell by 50 per cent to $0.03 billion in April and remained unchanged at $0.03 billion in May. Other Investments also fluctuated during the period. Inflows declined by 25 per cent MoM to $0.09 billion in February from $0.12 billion in January, before rising sharply by 77.8 per cent to $0.16 billion in March. The inflow subsequently fell by 12.5 per cent to $0.14 billion in April and declined further by 35.7 per cent to $0.09 billion in May. items.title: Parliament questions proliferation of unapproved containers in East Legon
items.description: Parliament’s Local Government and Rural Development Committee has challenged the Ayawaso West Municipal Assembly over the growing number of containers and temporary structures springing up across East Legon. The concern emerged when officials of the Assembly appeared before the Committee to account for development activities in the municipality, including the enforcement of physical planning and building regulations. Assembly officials told lawmakers that they had not authorised the containers and other temporary structures currently occupying various parts of East Legon. The disclosure prompted questions about how the structures were being erected and why they had remained in place despite the Assembly’s lack of approval. Committee members expressed concern that the situation could undermine orderly development in an area known for its high-value residential and commercial properties. They questioned the Assembly’s monitoring systems and its ability to enforce planning regulations effectively. Committee Chairperson Queenstar Maame Pokuah Sawyerr demanded action to prevent further proliferation of the structures. “Why do you allow containers springing up everywhere around such an expensive area? And temporary structures too. There are a lot of them there. Are you ready to do something about it because they are unauthorised structures and containers and all of that?” she asked. The Committee subsequently directed the Ayawaso West Municipal Assembly to develop a comprehensive plan to deal with the unauthorised structures and ensure that existing planning regulations are enforced. The directive is intended to prevent further encroachment and restore greater order to development within the municipality.

items.title: Yemen: Houthis Prosecute UN, Civil Society Staff
items.description: Click to expand Image A United Nations team visits with officials of Yemen's Supervisory Committee in Al Hudaydah province, Yemen, May 17, 2023. © 2023 Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images (Beirut) – The Houthi de facto authorities in Yemen have sent at least eight people involved in human rights and humanitarian work for criminal prosecution, on espionage-related charges punishable by death, since August 18, 2026, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch said today. They include two United Nations employees, a UN consultant, and five people who worked with international and local civil society organizations on a range of issues, including health, human rights, and humanitarian aid. The Houthis should immediately halt these prosecutions and unconditionally release the eight people whose cases were sent to the prosecution, as well as the scores of other UN staff and civil society workers the Houthis have arbitrarily detained over the past two years. The prosecution is the latest escalation in a crackdown by Houthi authorities on civil society in the part of Yemen they control, with successive waves of arrests of Yemenis targeting UN staff and civil society members since May 31, 2024. The Houthis have arbitrarily detained over 100 such staff and workers, holding them without charge and denying them access to lawyers and their families. Many of the detentions started as enforced disappearances. An enforced disappearance happens when a person is deprived of liberty and their detention is denied or their situation or whereabouts concealed, placing them outside the protection of the law. “As fighting once again escalates in Yemen, the Houthis have maliciously moved to prosecute at least eight UN and civil society workers on charges that could, if convicted, result in the death penalty,” said Diala Haidar, Yemen researcher at Amnesty International. “Demanding the immediate release of Yemen’s UN and civil society workers should be a top priority for governments, and not an afterthought.” Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International spoke to seven people with direct knowledge of the cases, including family members of those detained. All eight transferred for prosecution remain in detention and have deteriorating health conditions, including at least two who have diabetes and have not been able to get adequate medical care and one who is at risk of glaucoma. One has stomach cancer and has been undergoing chemotherapy while in detention. Some family members said the detainees told them they had been forced to confess to espionage charges under torture or threats of torture. Since 2015, Amnesty International has documented scores of cases in which Houthi authorities used spying charges to target political opponents and silence peaceful dissent. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have documented the Houthis’ use of torture to obtain confessions. “It is outrageous that detainees are facing the risk of the death penalty simply for providing medical and food assistance or promoting human rights, peace, and dialogue,” said Niku Jafarnia, Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch. “It is critical for other governments to step up diplomatic efforts to secure the release of the dozens of arbitrarily detained members of Yemen’s civil society and UN staff, especially considering the attacks prisons have faced in the conflict.” Imposing the death penalty after unfair proceedings makes its use as a punishment arbitrary and in violation of international legal standards, the organizations said. Further, under international human rights law, only the “most serious crimes” can legitimately attract the death penalty, which has been interpreted as limited to intentional killing. None of those facing prosecution have been accused of such actions. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch oppose the death penalty unconditionally, in any cases and under any circumstance. The eight people transferred to the Specialized Criminal Prosecution in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital, are facing charges of “espionage” and “aiding the enemy” (articles 127 and 128 of Yemen’s Penal Code), both punishable by death. The Specialized Criminal Prosecution has also made vague and overly broad accusations about the detainees’ humanitarian and human rights work, alleging that they had “hidden and malicious goals” as part of a premeditated plan to “destroy the values of society.” The Sanaa-based Specialized Criminal Court, established in 1999, has jurisdiction over a variety of security-related crimes and offenses deemed detrimental to state security and public interests. As the Houthis consolidated their control over territories, they also consolidated their control over the judiciary, and the court has been used as a tool for political repression. All eight detainees have been denied adequate access to their lawyers. Sami Kallabi, 41, who worked for the UN at the time of his arrest on June 6, 2024, has cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy at a military hospital. Despite his critical health situation, he has been denied family visits and the Houthi authorities are refusing to disclose where he is being held. Labib Shayef, 57, is a consultant also detained on June 6, 2024, from his office in Sanaa. Since then, he has only been allowed a single visit from his family, in August 2025. His health has severely deteriorated in detention. He has diabetes and contracted Hepatitis B in custody but has not been provided with adequate access to health care. Prosecutors have questioned him about his work with local and international organizations, including on gender and peace-related programs. At the time of his arrest, Dr. Ali Al-Mudhwahi was a UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) consultant and an adviser to the Houthi’s Ministry of Public Health and Population, his wife Safiah Mohammed told Human Rights Watch. The authorities have subjected him to “solitary confinement, torture, and severe psychological pressure” throughout his detention, his wife said he told her over the phone. The Houthis, who oppose vaccinations, have tried to force Al-Mudhwahi to say that vaccines are “nothing but espionage tools” and that he is “a spy recruited by the World Health Organization,” his wife said. Starting on May 31, 2024, the Houthis carried out a series of raids in areas under their control, arbitrarily detaining 13 UN staff and at least 50 staff from Yemeni and international civil society organizations. Since that time, the Houthis have arbitrarily detained dozens more UN staff and civil society workers. As of February 2026, at least 73 UN staff and dozens of humanitarian and civil society workers remained in Houthi detention, all of them Yemeni nationals. On February 11, 2025, an aid worker from the World Food Programme died in Houthi custody. His death heightens fears for the safety and well-being of others arbitrarily detained in Houthi-run detention centers, given the Houthis’ track record of torture and other ill-treatment of detainees. Many of those detained were arrested without being shown arrest warrants and were forcibly disappeared for months before their detention was acknowledged and whereabouts known. While some have received medical care, many have not, including some people with serious medical conditions.

items.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, October 6, 2026
items.description: The naira traded within a relatively narrow range against the US dollar on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, with the local currency quoted at about ₦1,332.90 per dollar in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM), while the parallel market rate stood around ₦1,357 per dollar. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) showed that the naira depreciated slightly at the official market, with the dollar rising to ₦1,332.90 from ₦1,332 recorded at the previous weekend’s close. In the parallel market, the naira appreciated to about ₦1,357 per dollar from ₦1,362 at the weekend, according to market data reported on Tuesday. The movement left the gap between the NFEM and parallel market rates at about ₦24.10 per dollar, narrower than the ₦30 spread recorded over the weekend. The latest figures indicate that the naira continues to trade with relatively limited volatility as foreign exchange liquidity and market conditions remain closely watched by businesses, investors and consumers. The CBN said its NFEM rate is derived using the volume-weighted average and serves as the official exchange rate for the day. At the parallel market, however, rates can vary depending on location, dealer and transaction size. As of Tuesday, October 6, the dollar was therefore selling for approximately ₦1,357 in the parallel market, compared with about ₦1,332.90 at the official NFEM window. The difference between both markets remains significantly narrower than the wide spreads recorded during periods of heightened foreign exchange pressure, reflecting the continued convergence of the official and parallel markets. items.title: Particle physics, astrophysics and 'invisibility cloak' tipped for physics Nobel
items.description: Research in particle physics, astrophysics or the invention of an “invisibility cloak” are some of the achievements that could be honoured when the Nobel physics prize is awarded Tuesday. The award, to be announced at 11:45 am in Stockholm, is the second Nobel of the season, after the Medicine Prize was awarded on Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. The researchers were honoured for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics, which involves controlling nerve signals with light. For the physics prize, commentators have for years speculated that metamaterials and Britain’s John B. Pendry, who has become famous for his “invisibility cloak” where light is bent around an object, are due for a nod. “Since the first breakthrough 20 years ago it has become a large, varied field of research,” Camilla Widebeck, a science producer for public broadcaster Sveriges Radio told AFP , adding that Pendry would likely be honoured alongside American David Smith. Other commentators have suggested Italian-American Federico Capasso — who is also often cited for contributing to the invention and development of the quantum cascade laser —could also be honoured in the field. Widebeck also speculated that this year’s prize could build on the 2010 prize, which honoured research into the material graphene — a one-atom thick layer of carbon arranged in a honeycomb pattern. Spain’s Pablo Jarillo-Herrero together with Canada’s Allan MacDonald and Israel’s Rafi Bistritzer could be honoured for work on twistronics, where two such layers are twisted together — producing superconductivity which has the potential to lead to an energy revolution. The trio won the 2020 Wolf Prize in Physics, and Widebeck noted Romanian-born US researcher Eva Andrei was also a favourite in the field. However, she also cautioned that many believed that it “will probably be another few years” before the Nobel committee recognises the work. Particle physics Research firm Clarivate, which predicts winners of the prize based on the number of citations, spotlighted Japan’s Chihaya Adachi along with Americans Stephen R. Forrest and Mark E. Thompson this year for their work on “ultrahigh-efficiency organic light-emitting diodes” (OLEDs) — used to produce better image quality in screens for smartphones, TVs and computers with lower energy consumption. Speaking to AFP , David Pendlebury, who heads research analysis at Clarivate, noted that many discoveries can fall into multiple categories and a prize for “OLEDs could be chemistry or it could be physics.” Clarivate also spotlighted Swiss-British researcher Nicola Spaldin for her theoretical work on “magnetoelectric multiferroics” and China’s Qikun Xue “for experimental observation of the quantum anomalous Hall Effect,” which both have an impact on making products more energy efficient. Hamish Johnston, online editor of science magazine Physics World, wrote in a blog post that based on recent winners “it appears that both condensed-matter physics, and particle and nuclear physics are due a prize.” One possibility then is a prize for CERN’s ATHENA and ALPHA collaborations, “who were the first to trap cold antihydrogen atoms and then study them in detail,” which would make Denmark-based American physicist Jeffrey Hangst — a founder of both collaborations - A likely laureate The science writer also noted that the jury could honour Belgian physicist Ingrid Daubechies, together with French mathematicians Stephane Mallat and Yves Meyer — a trio which Clarivate spotlighted last year — for something called wavelet theory. The theory impacts our daily lives through things such as image compression for pictures and videos on computers. Trump watching Widebeck also noted that it had been some time since the academy honoured discoveries in the field of space and astrophysics. “One name that appears in the speculation is Briton Martin Rees,” she said, noting he had previously served as Britain’s Astronomer Royal. In the past, work on the James Webb Space Telescope has also been buzzed about, as has research into how galaxies are formed — with the work of Mexican-British cosmologist Carlos Frenk, Argentinian astrophysicist Julio Navarro and British scientist Simon White highlighted. Last year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Briton John Clarke, Frenchman Michel Devoret and American John Martinis for putting quantum mechanics into action and enabling the development of all kinds of digital technology from cellphones to a new generation of computers. The physics prize will be followed by the chemistry on Wednesday. The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday and the perhaps most keenly anticipated award — the peace prize — is due on Friday. US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize — and Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal — and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again. The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.

items.title: Promotion arrears alone cannot end teachers’ strike — PRETAG
items.description: The Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG) says the government’s commitment to clear outstanding promotion arrears will not, on its own, be enough to bring an end to the nationwide teachers’ strike. The association says several demands contained in agreements with government remain unresolved, making it difficult for the teacher unions to suspend the industrial action based solely on assurances over the payment of arrears. Among the concerns is a 20% professional allowance which, according to PRETAG, has remained outstanding despite commitments made by successive administrations. The association says teachers are still waiting for concrete action on the allowance as well as other provisions contained in their collective agreement. PRETAG President King Ali Awudu recalled that the issue dates back several years, pointing to an announcement by former Education Minister Alex Tetteh-Enyo in 2009 that government intended to introduce the allowance for teachers. “We are in 2026, and we are talking about the same thing that His Excellency also promised,” he said. Mr Awudu maintained that the unions needed more than assurances on promotion arrears before reconsidering the strike. “Our collective agreement with government is not willing to give us anything. These last two have not been met,” he said. He acknowledged government’s decision to begin processing some outstanding promotion arrears and the commitment to complete the payments by October 30, but said the move did not resolve the broader issues underpinning the industrial action. “The idea of calling off the strike is such a difficult one,” Mr Awudu said, insisting that concrete steps on the outstanding demands would be necessary for the unions to reconsider their position. His comments follow an assurance from Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu that government would settle the outstanding promotion arrears by October 30. The Minister has pledged to take responsibility should the deadline not be met, but the teacher unions have maintained their strike pending action on their wider demands and conditions of service.

items.title: Ebi Bright alleges assault on driver in dispute with Tema Central MP
items.description: Tema Metropolitan Chief Executive Ebi Bright has alleged that a dispute with Tema Central Member of Parliament Charles Forson has escalated to the point where one of her drivers was assaulted during an attempt to engage the legislator. Ms Bright said the strained relationship had made it difficult for the Tema Metropolitan Assembly to coordinate development initiatives with the MP, with some projects allegedly being undertaken without adequate consultation and subsequently duplicating work planned by the Assembly. She told Parliament’s Local Government and Rural Development Committee that efforts to resolve the disagreement had been unsuccessful despite interventions from individuals, including members of Parliament’s leadership. She attributed the breakdown in relations to her decision not to approve the release of the MP’s share of the District Assemblies Common Fund. Ms Bright said she had made several attempts to establish direct communication with Mr Forson, including trying to reach him at Parliament. She alleged that the latest attempt resulted in her driver being physically assaulted. “I have with the support of other individuals, including some leadership in Parliament, made attempts to approach him. The last of such attempt was met with physical assault on my driver because we tried to reach him at Parliament and we couldn’t reach him,” she said. She said a subsequent attempt to meet the MP at his residence also proved unsuccessful, after which she sent a package to his office as a gesture of goodwill and an invitation to engage. Ms Bright alleged that a member of her staff was also assaulted during that process. The MCE said the matter had since been brought to the attention of parliamentary leadership, with efforts being made to mediate the disagreement and restore cooperation between the Tema Metropolitan Assembly and the Tema Central MP.

items.title: Cross River: Ritual killings resurface ahead of 2027 elections
items.description: By Emma Una Observations over the last 11 years have shown that in Cross River State, cases of alleged ritual killings tend to increase as general elections draw near, with women accounting for more than 90 per cent of the reported victims. Our Correspondent, Emma Una, highlights the ugly trend in the last decade. Since 2015, when the ugly trend reportedly began, several women have been killed, yet no alleged ritualist has been apprehended or any suspect arrested in connection with the killings. In many of the cases, the killers appear to leave little or no trail, while the victims are stripped of items or identifying details that could help investigators unravel the circumstances surrounding their deaths. With the 2027 elections approaching, there are already reported instances of women being found dead, with some of their vital body parts allegedly missing. The most recent case was the brutal murder of a woman at a guest house along Clifford Lane, Calabar South, on September 7, 2026. Her killer or killers allegedly removed anything that could provide investigators with a lead. To make matters worse, the hotel receptionist reportedly failed to record the personal details of the man with whom the woman allegedly checked into the hotel that night.When the man reportedly left the following morning, no one noticed him or could provide a useful description of his appearance. Some months earlier, another woman was killed in a hotel in Yahe, Yala Local Government Area, in the northern part of the state. She was allegedly lured to the hotel, but hotel staff reportedly failed to obtain the details of the man who accompanied her. In neighbouring Ogoja, another girl was reportedly lured to the outskirts of the town along the Ogoja-Katsina Ala road, where she was killed. Her private parts, tongue and other vital body parts were allegedly harvested before her body was abandoned by the roadside. In Ikom, a woman was killed along the Ikom-Obudu road, with her breast and tongue reportedly cut off. The killing generated widespread outrage in the area, but after the initial uproar, nothing concrete emerged from the investigation. Again, at Satellite Town, close to the University of Calabar Teaching Hospital, a woman was found dead and abandoned by the roadside. These are among the killings that have become known to the public. Yet, according to available accounts, none of the cases has resulted in the arrest of a suspect. In the latest incident, the Police appealed to members of the public to help identify the victim. In a statement, the Cross River State Police Public Relations Officer, Sunday Eitokpah, said: “The Cross River State Police Command wishes to provide an update on the ongoing investigation on the suspected homicide of an unidentified female guest at a hotel along Clifford Lane, Calabar South, earlier reported by the Police in its press release of 8 September, 2026.” He said preliminary investigations revealed that the deceased lodged at the hotel alongside a male guest whose whereabouts remained under investigation. According to him, efforts were ongoing to locate the man to establish the circumstances surrounding the woman’s death. The series of deaths has raised concern among residents and observers, particularly because the victims are predominantly young women. Some observers, however, have also expressed concern about the circumstances in which some of the victims reportedly meet the men who later become their last known companions. They argued that some women fail to inform friends or relatives about their movements or where they are going, making it difficult for families to raise the alarm or assist investigators when something goes wrong. “Ladies are too much in a hurry to hook up with people who lure them with flashy things. They fail to understand the present times where people are desperate for wealth,” Eyobam told NDV. As the 2027 elections draw closer, the latest incidents have revived fears among residents that a disturbing pattern of unexplained killings could once again be taking shape across the state. For the families of the victims, however, the most troubling question remains unanswered: who are the killers, and why have they continued to escape justice? items.title: GH¢35m Darkuman 24-hour market to be completed in 16 months — MCE
items.description: The Ablekuma North Municipal Assembly has begun construction of a GH¢35 million 24-hour market at Darkuman, with the facility expected to be completed within 16 months. Municipal Chief Executive Adamu Musah Kalamu said the project was intended to improve trading conditions while opening up new employment opportunities for residents in the municipality. He expressed confidence that the contractor would meet the agreed completion period and deliver a facility that would serve traders and residents. “It is our prayer and hope that the contractor, as stated in the contract, within 16 months will hand over the site, the completed market to the good people of Ablekuma North,” he said. Mr Musah Kalamu said local artisans, labourers, carpenters and other young people would be encouraged to take up employment opportunities created by the project. He appealed to residents to cooperate with the contractor and support the project to ensure its timely completion. “We want the community to give our contractors all the necessary support so that they will finish in record time,” he said. items.title: NPP risks losing Karaga seat if Amin Adam doesn’t contest – John Boadu
items.description: Newly elected National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, says the party risks losing the Karaga parliamentary seat if former Finance Minister and incumbent MP, Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, does not contest the constituency in the next election. According to him, the NPP must persuade Dr Amin Adam to seek another term in Parliament, describing his continued participation in the contest as important to the party’s prospects in Karaga. Speaking in an interview on Adom FM’s Dwaso Nsem on Monday, October 5, Mr Boadu said the party would have to “beg” Dr Amin Adam to contest again rather than allow him to step aside. “We will have to beg him to contest again. If he doesn’t contest, we will lose the seat,” Mr Boadu said. Dr Amin Adam has represented Karaga in Parliament since 2021 and remains the constituency’s current NPP MP. Official parliamentary records list him as the NPP’s representative for Karaga. Mr Boadu’s comments form part of his broader position that the NPP must take strategic decisions and make difficult choices as it prepares for the 2028 general election. He has said the party’s primary objective is to regain political power and that its decisions must ultimately serve that goal.

items.title: UN chief Guterres arrives in Pakistan for 2-day visit
items.description: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres arrived in Islamabad in the early hours of Tuesday for a two-day official visit, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The FO said the UN chief was visiting Pakistan from October 6 to 8 at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. “Upon arrival, the secretary-general was received by Acting Foreign Secretary Ambassador Nabeel Munir,” FO said in a post on social media platform X. The visit comes as Guterres’ 10-year tenure as UN chief is set to end on Dec 31. During the visit, Guterres is set to meet President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, as well as Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, the FO said on Monday. The UN chief is also scheduled to visit the headquarters of the United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) and attend a briefing at the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) headquarters. In its Monday statement, FO said that during Guterres’ visit, Pakistan’s “efforts towards strengthening multilateralism and international peace and security, as well as its strides towards disaster preparedness and early warning, will be highlighted”. It stated that the visit will offer an important opportunity to reiterate Pakistan’s longstanding cooperation with the UN and to exchange views on regional and international developments. PM Shehbaz met Guterres on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month. The two discussed major regional and international developments, including the situation in the Middle East. In that meeting, Guterres commended Pakistan’s role and strong voice at the UN, as well as its contribution to international peace and security. The UN chief also appreciated Pakistan’s role and sacrifices in countering terrorism. Guterres’ first visit to Pakistan as the UN secretary general was in February 2020, about three years after he was elected to the position in 2016. In recent months, two of the six candidates vying to succeed Guterres have visited Pakistan and met PM Shehbaz. items.title: Ghana Reference Rate falls to 10.04% in October as borrowing costs ease
items.description: The Ghana Reference Rate (GRR), the benchmark used by commercial banks to price loans, has fallen further to 10.04% in October 2026. The latest figure represents a decline from 10.18% recorded in September. The reduction, based on JOYBUSINESS calculations using the industry-approved formula and market data from industry players, points to a continued easing in the benchmark rate. Reasons The latest decline was largely influenced by slight reductions in Treasury bill (T-bill) rates and interbank market rates. This comes despite the Monetary Policy Rate remaining unchanged at 14% since the first quarter of 2026. The trend suggests that movements in the Ghana Reference Rate this year have been influenced more by fiscal and money-market conditions than changes in the central bank’s policy rate. T-bill rates, which reflect developments in government borrowing and fiscal conditions, have played a key role. Interbank market dynamics, including increased liquidity and competition among banks, have also contributed to the movement in the benchmark. Implications The marginal decline could offer some relief to borrowers with variable-rate loan facilities as lending costs continue to ease. Customers with fixed-rate loans, however, are unlikely to be immediately affected by the latest reduction. The development could also benefit new borrowers as banks compete to provide credit at lower rates. Average lending rates have fallen to around 15%, while some customers are reportedly accessing credit at rates between 11% and 12.5%. GRR Movement in 2026 The Ghana Reference Rate has recorded mixed movements throughout 2026. The benchmark stood at 11.71% in March before declining to 10.06% in April. It eased further to 10.03% in May and 10.02% in June before rising to 10.59% in July. The rate increased further to 10.61% in August, then fell to 10.18% in September and now to 10.04% in October. The latest movement therefore continues the recent downward trend in the benchmark. Background The Ghana Reference Rate was introduced in 2017 by the Bank of Ghana in collaboration with the Ghana Association of Banks. It was designed to provide a transparent and uniform benchmark for determining lending rates across Ghana’s banking sector. The benchmark is used by commercial banks as a key reference point when pricing loans and other credit facilities.

items.title: 53% of NPP delegates backed alternatives to John Boadu in chairmanship race – Mussa Dankwah
items.description: The outcome of the New Patriotic Party’s national chairmanship election has been interpreted as a sign that a significant number of the party’s delegates sought an alternative to John Boadu’s leadership. Although Mr Boadu emerged victorious at the party’s National Delegates Conference in Kumasi on October 3, the combined votes of the three other candidates exceeded his tally. The figures show Mr Boadu securing 2,888 votes, compared with 2,408 for Boakye Kyerematen Agyarko, 790 for Paul Afoko and 41 for Sammy Crabbe. The combined 3,239 votes secured by Mr Agyarko, Mr Afoko and Mr Crabbe represented about 53% of the votes cast, while Mr Boadu’s 2,888 votes accounted for about 47%. The analysis suggests that the result was not simply a straightforward endorsement of one candidate, but also reflected different expectations among delegates about the direction of the party and the kind of leadership they wanted. Speaking on Channel One TV on Monday, October 5, Executive Director of Global InfoAnalytics Mussa Dankwah said the voting pattern indicated that delegates who supported the unsuccessful candidates were looking for a different type of leadership. “I think there were people who wanted men with stature for chairman,” he said, adding that the demographic of delegates who backed Paul Afoko was similar to that of those who supported Boakye Agyarko. Mr Dankwah also argued that the desire for unity may have helped Mr Boadu secure the chairmanship, despite the combined strength of the other candidates. “You can say that more people wanted unity; therefore, they chose John Boadu,” he said. Mr Boadu is now expected to lead the party’s national reorganisation as the NPP begins preparations for the 2028 general elections, following his election as National Chairman.

items.title: High taxes, water shortages push up hotel operating costs — Hotels Association
items.description: Hotel operators are warning of growing pressure on the hospitality industry as rising taxes, utility bills and other operational expenses make it increasingly difficult to keep accommodation costs affordable. The situation is particularly challenging in parts of the Central Region, where some hotels in Elmina have reportedly had to rely on water tankers after experiencing prolonged interruptions in their regular water supply. The additional cost of securing water, according to the Ghana Hotels Association, is adding to an already difficult operating environment, with hotels having to provide water for rooms and facilities such as swimming pools from alternative sources. President of the Ghana Hotels Association, Victor Minta, said the situation in Elmina had persisted for nearly three months, forcing hotels to spend heavily on tanker services. “Currently, the cost of business is very high, such that in the Central Region, in Elmina specifically, for nearly three months, there’s been no water flowing through the taps,” he said. Mr Minta also raised concerns about the tax burden on hotels, explaining that a sizeable share of revenue from room sales is absorbed by taxes before operators meet their other business expenses. “Every hotel room you sell at approximately 100 cedis, about 20 percent is taxes. So even you have about 80 cedis left to cater for the cost of actually doing business,” he said. Despite the cost pressures, the association says hotels are preparing promotional offers ahead of the festive season in an effort to attract more guests and encourage longer stays. Proposed packages include offers where visitors who book several nights receive an additional night at no extra cost. “We’re looking at how to provide promotions that provide maybe three or four nights and the fifth night free, that kind of thing, to help encourage more people to travel, to escape and to rejuvenate,” Mr Minta said.

items.title: Catholic Bishops demand tougher action on tramadol, marijuana and other drugs
items.description: The Ghana Catholic Bishops’ Conference is urging authorities to widen the country’s approach to tackling drug abuse, warning that substances readily available in communities are taking a serious toll on young people. The Bishops say the national response must go beyond the fight against cocaine and other high-profile narcotics to include drugs that are more easily obtained and widely used by young people. They are particularly concerned about the growing use of tramadol, marijuana, “Red” and other substances, which they say are contributing to the destruction of the lives and prospects of many young people in communities across the country. President of the Ghana Catholic Bishops’ Conference, Most Rev. Matthew Gyamfi, told Citi FM that the scale of abuse of readily accessible drugs required urgent attention. He argued that authorities should strengthen laws and enforcement to restrict the importation and illegal sale of such substances and remove them from the shelves. Most Rev. Gyamfi said the focus on cocaine alone risked overlooking substances that were being consumed more extensively by young people. “You should not concentrate only on drugs like cocaine, which is used, but not as massively as marijuana, tramadol, ‘Red’ and other similar drugs that are readily available on the shelves, and young people just go for it,” he stated. He called for stronger measures to prevent the importation and distribution of the drugs, while urging authorities to intensify efforts to protect young people from substance abuse and address the wider social consequences of the drug menace.

items.title: Taps run dry in Karachi's Clifton, Defence as official tanker service faces delays
items.description: KARACHI: Residents of Clifton and Defence, who rely on water tankers, have been facing difficulty in getting a bowser from the Cantonment Board Clifton (CBC) as its tanker service is facing delays due to an acute shortage. At a recent meeting between the CBC and the Clifton Defence Community (CDC), a detailed discussion was held on the acute water shortage faced by the residents, a Rs14 billion project to lay a new waterline dedicated from Dumlottee to DHA and pending tanker supply applications. When many residents, who attended the meeting, complained that they are not even getting water through the CBC tankers despite having been given out tokens, it was explained that owing to the current shortage, the tanker supply is two to three months behind schedule. The residents suggested that the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation water tankers be diverted to DHA too to take care of the backlog in supplying water as they are also available at a relatively lower price than the private tankers and can be booked a few days in advance. In meeting with residents, CBC officials attribute backlog in bowser supply to water shortage In a bid to learn more about the proposed dedicated waterline project, CDC President Abdur Rehman inquired about its progress from CBC officials, including Secretary Sajjad Nazir and Chief Cantonment Engineer Abdul Rahim Shaikh. It was explained that work on the new pipeline, expected to complete in a year’s time, has already started. The pipeline will carry unfiltered water from Dumlottee, which will then be purified through filtration plants before being supplied to the residents through their lines. The residents also requested that the existing water distribution system be improved before the new project is completed. There were other complaints also raised by residents about private tankers filling up from CBC hydrants to which the CBC officials denied any such action. They further said that if any resident saw a private tanker filling water from a CBC hydrant, they should take a picture of it and immediately send it to the CBC officials concerned so that the matter can be investigated and necessary action be taken. “There are unnecessary and redundant lines and ineffective management of valves that need to be looked into,” said CDC’s President Abdur Rehman. He also highlighted the residents’ suggestion of installing water meters and devising an effective system for supply according to water consumption, so that the internal system is fully ready by the time the water supply from the new line begins. Regarding residents’ concerns over tanker service delays, CBC Secretary Nazir told Dawn: “We facilitated those [residents] at the meeting who showed us their tokens [for water tankers] on a priority basis the very same day.” Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

items.title: After two crisis-ridden years, Pakistan’s UN envoy heads home to take up foreign secretary mantle
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad leaves New York this week to take up his new responsibilities as Pakistan’s foreign secretary, ending his two-year assignment as the country’s permanent representative to the United Nations (UN). He arrived in New York in October 2024 for his third assignment at the United Nations, as Pakistan prepared to begin a two-year elected term on the UN Security Council (UNSC). It was his third consecutive term as part of Pakistan’s UNSC teams, following assignments in 2003-04 and 2012-13. “It is such a great and singular honour to have the opportunity to represent Pakistan at the UN, including at the Security Council,” Ahmad said in an interview with Dawn . His tenure unfolded amid an extraordinary succession of crises: last year’s brief military confrontation between India and Pakistan, the continuing catastrophe in Gaza, the war between Israel and Iran and growing divisions within the international system. Pakistan brought “a lot of expertise and institutional experience” to its eighth term on the UNSC, Ahmad said. Its priorities were focused on international peace and security, including conflict prevention and peaceful settlement of disputes, peacekeeping, counter-terrorism and cooperation with regional organisations, he added. Within months of his arrival, relations between Pakistan and India deteriorated sharply, leading to a four-day military confrontation in May 2025 that brought the two nuclear-armed neighbours dangerously close to a wider conflict. The UN repeatedly urged both sides to step back from the brink and offered its good offices to help de-escalate the crisis. Ahmad kept UNSC members and other UN delegations informed of Pakistan’s position and the dangers of further escalation. Pakistan and India agreed to a ceasefire on May 10. For Ahmad, the confrontation was particularly significant because Pakistan itself was serving on the UNSC. In assessing Pakistan’s subsequent emphasis on peaceful settlement, he pointed to the May 2025 conflict, saying Pakistan had initiated and steered a UNSC resolution after “having inflicted a crushing defeat to the Indian aggression in May 2025.” One of the principal results he cited was UNSC Resolution 2788, adopted unanimously during Pakistan’s presidency in July 2025. The Pakistan-sponsored resolution called for greater use of the mechanisms provided by the UN Charter for the peaceful settlement of disputes. Ahmad described it as a landmark resolution, saying it had been “the most widely referred UNSC decision” since its adoption, something he said testified to its importance and relevance to the council’s work. Despite the geopolitical tensions reflected in a polarised council, he said, Pakistan had been able to forge consensus around the resolution. He also used his assessment of Pakistan’s tenure to argue for reform of the UNSC. Ahmad said developments in the international peace and security landscape, together with growing criticism of the role of the permanent members, had reinforced the belief of a wide majority of UN member states that the council needed to become “more democratic, representative and accountable”. Adding new individual permanent members, he argued, would only aggravate the problem. “In simple words, the problem cannot be the solution,” he said. Pakistan, he added, had worked with its partners in the Uniting for Consensus group and other like-minded countries for a reformed council with more elected seats, including medium-term seats based on periodic elections and rotation. Such an arrangement, he said, would allow for representation and accountability corresponding to the realities of today’s world. “Pakistan and many other countries are eminently qualified to bring their contribution to the UNSC and the maintenance of international peace and security,” Ahmad said. “Member states should be ready to fulfil that responsibility without permanence and privilege,” he said. Gaza became another defining issue of his tenure. Pakistan repeatedly raised the Palestinian question at the UNSC and the General Assembly, calling for an end to the killing and humanitarian suffering and adherence to international law. Ahmad described Pakistan as a “forceful voice” on Palestine. He pointed to Pakistan’s support for the Comprehensive Plan on Gaza and Security Council Resolution 2803, which he said brought about a ceasefire, opened humanitarian space in Gaza and, importantly, restored a political horizon for Palestinian self-determination and statehood. The Israel-Iran war in June 2025 and subsequent direct US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities presented Pakistan with another delicate diplomatic challenge. Iran is Pakistan’s neighbour, and Ahmad said Pakistan played an important role in mediating between the United States and Iran, bringing about a ceasefire in April , the Islamabad talks and the process that led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June 2026. “Our leadership remains closely engaged with all sides and other friends and partners to advance the prospects of peace,” he said. The episode illustrated another aspect of Pakistan’s diplomacy during Ahmad’s tenure: efforts to create space for dialogue beyond formal UN forums. Pakistan also used its UNSC membership to focus on the safety of UN peacekeepers. Together with Denmark, it led Resolution 2823 in June 2026 on accountability for attacks against UN peacekeepers. The resolution was adopted unanimously and attracted 153 co-sponsors from across the UN membership — a record number for a UNSC resolution on the issue, according to Ahmad. Kashmir remained another longstanding issue on Pakistan’s diplomatic agenda. Several Arria Formula meetings organised by Pakistan brought the Jammu and Kashmir dispute before the council. Ahmad said the meetings brought into focus the unresolved dispute and “the imperative of its peaceful settlement in accordance with international legitimacy and relevant UNSC resolutions.” Beyond the major conflicts, Pakistan maintained an active profile across the wider UN agenda, including UN80, development, climate change and emerging technologies. Ahmad cited Pakistan’s role in discussions on artificial intelligence, digital assets and tokenisation for development, saying Pakistan had taken the lead in pioneering discussion of these issues at the UN. He also pointed to Pakistan’s work in steering the first General Assembly resolution on access to assistive technologies. But much of the work of a permanent representative takes place away from the headlines: consultations with other missions, negotiations over the language of resolutions, briefings for visiting leaders and long discussions over individual words. His final major assignment was the 81st General Assembly in September. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and his delegation came to New York for the Assembly. Ahmad led the Pakistani Mission through the programme of meetings, briefings and the Prime Minister’s address. On September 10, Ahmad was designated Pakistan’s next foreign secretary. He paid his farewell call on UN Secretary General António Guterres on September 30. Guterres thanked Pakistan for its role at the United Nations and congratulated Ahmad on his new appointment. On October 3, the Pakistan Mission held a farewell for Ahmad and his family. Mission officers, Consulate General officials and their families attended the event. Ahmad leaves New York after a period marked by war, confrontation and intense diplomatic uncertainty, but also after Pakistan sought to use its UNSC seat to promote peaceful settlement of disputes, protect UN peacekeepers and press for a more representative Council. Now, he returns to Islamabad as foreign secretary.

items.title: Government positioning Banda District to become major tourism destination hub – Housing Minister
items.description: Ahmed Ibrahim, the Minister of Works, Housing and Water Resources, says the Banda District in the Bono Region would become a major tourism destination hub in the country within the next five years. He said the government was working tirelessly to develop the district’s rich tourism attraction sites, saying that the ongoing physical infrastructure development would well position the district to become a tourist destination in the country and even beyond. Mr Ibrahim, also the Member of Parliament (MP) for Banda Constituency said this when he inspected the progress of work on the construction of some physical infrastructure projects in the district as part of his “Accounting to the people” to the district. He stressed that Banda was endowed with several tourist attraction sites, like the Hippo Sanctuary, Bui National Park, Bui Hydro Lake, the Spider Village, as well as interesting archaeological sites and caves and mountains. “Banda has the natural tourist attraction sites, and we are developing the required physical and artificial tourist facilities,” Mr Ibrahim stated. Besides, he noted that the district offered significant opportunities for renewable energy development, saying that a floating solar project at the Bui Generating Station (BGS) could further enhance the tourism potential in the area. Mr Ibrahim inspected works on a modern community social centre and artificial pitch projects, saying that those projects were about 90 perccent. “There is a lot of tourism potential here, and in the next few years those potentials will all take shape,” he added. Mr Joseph Addae Akwaboa, the Bono Regional Minister, expressed excitement about the number of physical infrastructure projects being undertaking in the district, saying that the area had witnessed improvements in infrastructure development. Some of these facilities include police stations, classroom blocks, teachers’ accommodation, health centres, nurses’ quarters and water and sanitation facilities, spread across the various communities in the district.

items.title: Deputy Education Minister appeals to striking teachers to return to classrooms
items.description: Dr Clement Apaak, a Deputy Minister of Education, has appealed to striking pre-tertiary teachers to return to the classroom while government works to resolve their outstanding concerns. He said the government recognised the legitimacy of the teachers’ demands and was committed to addressing issues relating to their promotions, salary adjustments, allowances, rural and underserved community incentives, and conditions of service. Dr Apaak made the appeal at Bolgatanga during the 5th Upper East Regional Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Awards ceremony, where 15 journalists were recognised for their contributions to journalism. He explained that the delay in implementing new salary scales and consequential allowances for nearly 80,000 teachers who had passed promotional examinations, was partly because of the challenges in transferring the relevant data from the Ghana Education Service (GES) to the Controller and Accountant-General’s Department. The government had earlier agreed that promotions would be made automatic and that teachers would not be required to submit input forms, payslips and promotional letters before receiving their new salary scales and allowances. Dr Apaak said. He said the government had also agreed that the affected teachers would receive the new salaries and allowances with effect from January 2026, regardless of whether they wrote the promotional examinations in December 2025 or January 2026. On the proposed 20 per cent-plus salary incentive for teachers posted to rural, underserved and deprived communities, Dr Apaak said the government had assured the teacher unions that its implementation would begin next year. However, the government was working to clearly define which communities qualified as rural, underserved and deprived to ensure that the policy was implemented fairly. He said the issue also involved determining what would happen to a teacher’s entitlement when the teacher was transferred from a qualifying community. The Deputy Minister said the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission had been engaged to meet the leadership of the teacher unions, while President John Dramani Mahama had also directed a high-level meeting involving the Ministers of Finance, Labour Relations and Employment, Education and the teacher unions to continue the negotiations. “We want to encourage you to continue,” appealing to the teachers to return to the classroom as the government worked to resolve the outstanding issues. “We can be assured that what is due them, no matter how long it takes, it will come for their arrears,” Dr Apaak said. Dr Apaak stated that the government was concerned about the impact of the strike on pupils and students, stressing that teachers remained central to the development of the country. He said the absence of teachers from classrooms could undermine efforts at providing quality education and urged all parties to work together to resolve the impasse. “Without the teachers, we would not be here,” he said, describing teachers as “the most important group of professionals.” The 5th Upper East Regional GJA Awards, held under the theme, “Beyond the Headlines: The Media’s Role in Promoting WASH for Safe Motherhood and Quality Healthcare.” The awards ceremony was supported by Lesken Enterprise Ltd, Myturn Limited, KacStone Records, Paga Youth Movement, NorthLite Solar Ltd, ActionAid Ghana, Afrikids Ghana, NABOCADO, Endswell Pharmacy, MTN, Alafia, WaterAid Ghana, Widows and Orphans Movement, Ghana Tourism Authority, Ghana Hotels Association and AquaBolg Natural Water.

items.title: Government to involve corporate Ghana in street maintenance – Ayariga
items.description: The Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, has announced the commencement of a new programme where corporate organisations will partner with the State to clean, green, light, and maintain major streets in the major cities across the country. Mr Mahama Ayariga, the Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, made the disclosure on Monday, when he took his turn at the Government Accountability Series Press Conference held at the Presidency. He said under the direction of President John Dramani Mahama, they had commenced an exercise to assign all streets in the nation’s major capital cities to private businesses, including banks, manufacturing companies, construction firms, logistics companies and insurance firms. Mr Ayariga said they assumed responsibility for the reconstruction, redevelopment, and maintenance of those streets, renaming those streets after the companies or sharing the names with existing name personalities, and advertising rights along those streets, motivational considerations that we will infuse into the design of the programme. Taking the Obasanjo Highway as an example, he said the Access Bank would be given the mandate to redevelop the street, make sure that it was maintained and well lit, and ensure adequate greenery, as well as ensure that the walkways were always paved and safe. Mr Ayariga said he would have a meeting on Tuesday, October 6 with the Governor of the Central Bank, with all heads of the financial institutions. He said the Governor himself had expressed readiness to mobilise the banks to actively adopt streets and fix them. “The initiative will be rolled out in the coming days and weeks. The first report on the initiative is expected from the Chief Executive of the Land Use and Spatial Planning Authority. Mr Ayariga also announced that President John Dramani Mahama had also directed that he produced a strategy for building adequate inner-city infrastructure, such as adequate roads and drains in every neighbourhood in cities across the country. He said the President was leading a discussion involving himself (Mr Ayariga), Mr Kwami Governs Agbodza, the Minister for Roads and Highways and Dr Cassiel Ato Baah Forson, the Finance Minister, to develop an inner-city Big Push Initiative to redevelop the nation’s inner cities. Mr Ayariga said the initiative would be largely funded by a carefully reconfigured property-red regime and betterment charges with government support. He said that basically what they plan to do, the full details would be announced by the President in due course. “The objective is to ensure every neighbourhood in our cities has paved routes, paved streets, walkways, adequate drainage, street lighting, and enough greenery,” he said. “We ask for the cooperation of all property owners when we commence work. The values of your properties will be considerably enhanced by the end of completion of this initiative.” He said, he knew that several home owners wanted their neighbourhoods to be developed by Regimamuel Gray and Trassaco Estates respectively. He reiterated that they just needed the leadership of the Government to facilitate that, which was basically what the scheme was going to enable.

items.title: No contractor is untouchable because of political links — Agbodza
items.description: Engineers overseeing government road projects have been challenged to put professional standards ahead of political considerations and take firm action against contractors who fail to deliver according to their contracts. The Roads and Highways Minister, Governs Kwame Agbodza, said project supervisors must have the confidence to enforce specifications and timelines without being influenced by the political or personal connections of contractors. He warned that engineers should not hesitate to sanction or demand corrective action from contractors simply because they are believed to be close to senior government officials. According to him, such perceptions must not undermine the professional responsibilities of engineers tasked with protecting the quality of public infrastructure. “There was a culture where maybe engineers felt that contractor A is a friend of the minister or the president. If I go hard on him or her, they will report me and something will happen to me and that is why you hear me saying that no contractor is bigger than the smallest engineer supervising you,” he said. Speaking to Citi FM, Mr Agbodza said engineers should apply the same professional standards to every contractor, regardless of their relationship with government officials. “Even if my mother is a contractor, you are overseeing. Deal with him or her in the way that is within your professional view,” he stated. He added that neither his own connections nor those of the President should give any contractor the freedom to disregard contractual obligations. “I don’t think there is any contractor closer to me or the president or anybody who has got the licence to do the wrong thing or delay any project,” he said. The Minister’s comments highlight the role of independent and effective supervision in ensuring that government road projects meet agreed specifications, quality standards and delivery timelines.

items.title: The Rise of Gig Economy Warfare
Contractors to resume work on Phase Two of Kejetia Market Project
items.description: Mahama Ayariga, the Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs has announced that in the coming weeks, contractors will resume work on Phase Two of the Kumasi Market Project (Kejetia Market). He said negotiations had been completed to get the contractors back to site for the completion of the Kumasi Central Market, popularly called the Kejetia Market Phase Two. He recalled that after completing Phase One, the next Phase was left with about 60 per cent to be completed but had stalled for the past two years. Mr Ayariga made the revelation in his address at the Government Accountability Series Press Conference held on Monday at the Presidency. He said some negotiations had been made with the contractor, and Dr Cassiel Ato Baah Forson, the Minister of Finance, had given them approval to commence work on Phase Two. Additionally, the Finance Minister had given his approval for the use of proceeds from Phase One and Phase Two to get the contractors to commence work on Phase Three. He said the contractors would be moving back to site very shortly to begin work, while negotiations continued regarding the pricing of Phase Three and the mode of financing. Mr Ayariga said, he would continue the discussions that had started with the Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly, the Ashanti Regional Coordinating Council and the Asantehene Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, to see how to go about implementing the Phase Three. He assured residents of Kumasi and Ashanti Region that very soon the contractor would be back to site to continue with the work. He said the same contractor would also present to them a plan of how to commence the development of Phase Three. Mr Ayariga said the Finance Minister had revealed to him an ambitious programme of market development across the country, which he would announce in the 2027 budget. He said, it was his intention to explore finance options for other markets across their various regional capitals. He noted that their commitment to market rate development across the country stands for the push for an economy that runs hours, to create jobs and improve the conditions under which mothers spent most of their weekdays. He said this was a pro-women’s government that was concerned about the welfare of women. Mr Ayariga said building on the ongoing rollout of the modern markets in Metropolitan Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs), assemblies would be guided to integrate local economic development into their planning and budgeting processes, partner with the private sector and development partners, to unlock local economic potentials. He announced that they had planned in consultation with the Minister of Finance, to appoint Regional Economists in every region to guide MMDAs in their economic development strategies. The various special development frameworks developed by the Land Use and Special Planning Authority provided economic blueprints for every MMDA, with studies showing the economic potential of every region and district. “The use of the 24-Hour Economy Markets has tended to create the impression that the whole thing about Government’s flagship programme of 24-Hour Economy is about markets.” He said he had therefore redesignated the initiative as District Economy Markets, to ensure that every district got a model market. The Minister said the projects had been rescoped into two phases, with the First Phase effectively delivering market stores, sheds and essential commercial spaces, whereas a second phase would provide the social amenities such as police and fire stations, and other social amenities that had been incorporated into the building. He said they had set up a committee to review the pace of work, and contractors who displayed lack of capacity would have their contracts terminated and reassigned to more competent companies. Mr Ayariga said funding for phase one was readily available for those who complete their contracts.

items.title: Government committed to resolving teachers’ concerns - Vice President
items.description: Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang says ongoing engagements with teacher unions are making progress towards resolving concerns that triggered industrial action. She said the discussions had been constructive and expressed hope that they would soon result in an agreement. Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said this on Monday at the Ghana Teacher Prize Awards ceremony in Accra, where outstanding teachers were honoured for their contribution to education and national development. She said addressing challenges confronting teachers was critical to strengthening the education system, while urging teachers to uphold professional and ethical standards. “Teachers have responsibilities under the National Teachers’ Standards, the Ghana Education Service Code of Conduct, and the professional and ethical standards of the National Teaching Council. “Government also has a responsibility to address challenges confronting the teaching profession and the education sector,” she said. The Vice President said the education sector continued to face challenges including career progression, recruitment and infrastructure deficits, particularly at the secondary-school level. She said more than GH¢33 billion had been allocated to education in the 2026 Budget to support infrastructure, textbooks, teaching and learning materials and teacher accommodation. Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said the allocation would support completion of 30 E-block projects and construction of new primary, junior high and kindergarten schools. “It would also provide textbooks and other teaching and learning materials, while measures were being implemented to improve access to accommodation for teachers,” she said. She said the Teacher Housing Initiative and 404-unit teacher bungalows in underserved communities were among measures to improve teachers’ living conditions. Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said 99 double-track schools had been converted to single-track institutions, adding that the government remained committed to eliminating the double-track system. She said the removal of the link between teachers’ promotion and administrative vacancies had enabled eligible teachers to progress through their professional ranks without waiting for positions to become available. The reform, the Vice President said, had increased the number of cases requiring validation and processing, while measures had been taken to address delays and pay outstanding entitlements. She said support for teachers should also include professional development as artificial intelligence, digital technologies and changing labour markets reshaped the world of work. “Government would therefore continue to invest in teacher education, in-service training and digital resources to equip teachers with the knowledge and skills required to prepare young people for the changing world,” she said. The Vice President congratulated recipients of the Ghana Teacher Prize, describing them as teachers who had distinguished themselves through knowledge, professionalism, dedication and commitment to their pupils and the teaching profession. She commended teachers across the country for their contribution to education and national development, particularly those working under challenging conditions. The Ghana Teacher Prize is an annual initiative that recognises teachers for excellence, professionalism and dedication in the delivery of education. Ms Abigail Agyeiwaa, an English teacher at Mangoase Senior High School, emerged as the overall outstanding teacher for 2026. She received a three-bedroom house valued at GH¢700,000 as her prize.
