items.title: Technical problem, not weather, may have caused Ondo aircraft crash — Gov Aiyedatiwa
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa said a possible technical or mechanical fault and the subsequent loss of signal may have caused the Nigerian Air Force aircraft crash in Igbokoda, ruling out bad weather as a likely factor. Aiyedatiwa spoke on Monday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today, hours after the Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State. The aircraft was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when it crashed in a swampy area opposite the Naval Base in Igbokoda. The Nigerian Air Force subsequently activated a search-and-rescue operation. Aiyedatiwa said the aircraft could have developed a fault while in the air, leading to the loss of communication with the control tower. He said, “It is not a case of wanting to land like I said. So, some kind of technical problem might have happened to the aircraft that would make it lose signal. Anything could have happened in terms of a mechanical issue; it is not a case of weather because if it is weather, they would not even take off in the first place, or maybe some weather along the line after they might have taken off. “From what we heard, from Benin to Lagos is not a long distance so if the weather was bad, it would no have taken off in the first place, they will wait until the weather is okay so probably, some aircraft must have developed fault in the air and for them to lose signal from the control tower and then, something might have gone wrong.” The governor, however, said there were no survivors yet, based on the information available to him. “So painful,” Aiyedatiwa said when asked about the incident. “No survivor yet, from the information I have gotten.” The crash occurred on Monday morning after the aircraft, with tail number NGR 931, disappeared from radio contact while en route from Benin to Lagos. Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said air traffic controllers had been unable to contact the aircraft by radio before information later confirmed it had crashed near the Naval Base in Igbokoda. He said preliminary information indicated that 25 passengers and seven crew members were on board, while the wreckage had been located and search-and-rescue operations were ongoing. Earlier, the NAF confirmed that the aircraft was an ATR-42 and said it was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when the accident occurred. The force said it was conducting search-and-rescue operations in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies. The post Technical problem, not weather, may have caused Ondo aircraft crash — Gov Aiyedatiwa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nana Akomea denies boycotting NPP swearing-in after third-place finish
items.description: Newly elected NPP Third Vice Chairperson Nana Akomea has denied claims that he deliberately boycotted the party’s swearing-in ceremony after finishing third in the election. Nana Akomea said his absence was due to traffic and not disappointment over the election result. He said he arrived at the venue shortly after the ceremony had ended. “I got there 10 minutes after the swearing-in.” Akomea said he was not even present when voting ended or during the collation and counting of results. “They had just introduced the witness and done the swearing. Actually, when we entered the stadium, we heard because we could hear to the radio that the swearing was going on.” He said he only knew the outcome after arriving at the venue and receiving information from his agents. “Oh, my agents were there, and then when I got there, the swearing had been done. So I knew I had taken the third position, and I was rushing to go for the swearing-in.” Akomea also explained the absence of fellow candidate Nana B, saying the two had been caught in traffic. “I don’t know. I think Nana B was caught up in the same traffic.” He dismissed suggestions that the absence of the two candidates was linked to the election outcome. “We were… I don’t understand how that could happen. Total falsehood.” Akomea said he saw Nana B when the candidates were introduced but did not see him again until the following afternoon. “In fact, I saw Nana B when we were introduced as candidates. After that, I didn’t see him again until the next afternoon on Sunday.” Although he arrived after the ceremony, Nana Akomea said he remained at the stadium. When told that he had therefore not yet been formally sworn in, Akomea said he expected the situation to be resolved. “Well, remember there’s an American president who had to be sworn in twice, so that is not new. We have our first meeting as a new executive, and I’m sure I’ll get myself sworn in.” Akomea admitted that the third-place finish disappointed him, although he said his campaign message had been well received. “Oh, because, as I said, my message was well received.” He said he had expected to finish higher despite joining the race late. “Yes, even though I had come in late, many of the delegates expressed disappointment that I had come in late.” Akomea also acknowledged the possibility that campaign spending may have played a role in the outcome. “Let’s be honest about that. Were you outspent? It’s possible, and it’s also possible that I also outspent somebody.”

items.title: Ghana, Egypt explore fresh avenues in defense, pharmaceuticals, and infrastructure
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi have reaffirmed the longstanding historic ties between their two nations, pledging to deepen cooperation across key strategic sectors, including trade, security, pharmaceuticals and infrastructure development. A statement issued by Ghana’s Presidency, said the two leaders made the commitment during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Eighth African Union (AU) Mid-Year Coordination Summit, held alongside the maiden Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt. Reflecting on the foundational bond between their countries, President Mahama and President El-Sisi recalled the Pan-African vision established during the era of Ghana’s first President, Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah, and Egypt’s former President, Gamal Abdel Nasser. It said both leaders agreed that building on the historic foundation remained vital for addressing contemporary regional development goals. President Mahama thanked Egypt for supporting Ghana’s resolution on reparations at the United Nations and urged that it maintain its backing as the international dialogue continued. To boost bilateral trade, the two leaders discussed concrete steps to strengthen political consultations and expand commercial activities. A key area of focus was the pharmaceutical sector, with discussions centered on streamlining and facilitating the registration of Egyptian pharmaceutical products in Ghana, to improve healthcare access and foster investment. Defense and regional security were also major agenda items. President Mahama expressed Ghana’s desire to expand security collaboration with Egypt, citing the North African nation’s advanced defense industry as a valuable model. He called for broader cooperation, particularly in intelligence sharing, capacity building, and counter-terrorism initiatives. The bilateral discussions further covered support for the Sahel-Gulf of Guinea Accord and the development of social housing. Looking to the future of urban planning, President Mahama revealed Ghana’s interest in learning from Egypt’s technical experience in developing mega-infrastructure projects. Specifically, Ghana aims to draw insights from Egypt’s execution of its New Administrative Capital as the country advanced its own strategic plans for a new capital city.

items.title: CSOs call for review of gold reconnaissance activities along Ghana’s inshore waters
items.description: A Coalition of Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) working in the area of fisheries and marine ecosystems, has petitioned the government to review and clarify legal agreements permitting GoldCoast Resource Corp to undertake offshore gold reconnaissance activities along Ghana’s inshore waters. In a statement copied to the Ghana News Agency (GNA), the Coalition said it had taken note of reports that the GoldCoast Resource Corp. Held ten offshore reconnaissance licences covering approximately 10,000 square kilometres, extending along about 300 kilometres of Ghana’s coastline between Half Assini in the Western, and Winneba in the Central regions, and reaching about 33 kilometres offshore. It said though they did not oppose responsible investment or the lawful use of Ghana’s natural resources, their concern was that decisions affecting the ocean space must protect fisheries, biodiversity, food security, human rights, and coastal livelihoods. According to the Coalition, the company’s published map indicated that substantial portions of its licensed area fell within Ghana’s Inshore Exclusion Zone (IEZ), which the Fisheries and Aquaculture Act, 2025 (Act 1146) defined as the coastal waters between the coastline and 12 nautical miles offshore. It said: “Company disclosures indicate that approximately 50,000 line-kilometres of airborne magnetic data have already been collected across 100 per cent of the licensed area, with more detailed work focused on a 500 square kilometres priority area encompassing the mouth of the Ankobra River. “The stated forward programme includes marine bathymetric and seismic surveys, followed by vibro-core drilling and bulk seabed sampling, but the company acknowledges that no mineral resource or reserve, or economic viability, has yet been established.” The Coalition noted that Ghana, therefore, still had an important opportunity to determine the legal, environmental, and social implications before authorising any further phase. It called on the government to clarify the legal position, stating that Section 32(3) of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), as amended, prohibited the holder of a reconnaissance licence from drilling or excavating. “More fundamentally, section 99(6) of Act 703, as amended, makes it an offence to use a floating platform or other equipment for mining or dredging to obtain minerals in Ghana’s natural water bodies, including the territorial sea, exclusive economic zone and continental shelf,” it added. It said Ghana’s expanded IEZ, the Marine Fisheries Management Plan, and the recently declared Marine Protected Area (MPA) in the Greater Cape Three Points enclave were important national commitments that should be considered together with any mineral decisions affecting the same waters. The Coalition said: “Taken together, the scale of the licences permitting GoldCoast Resource Corp.’s exclusive right to conduct offshore reconnaissance activities, their proximity to the coast, their intersection with the extended IEZ, the centrality of artisanal fisheries, the unresolved legal questions, and the proposed progression to intrusive seabed activity require that the facts and safeguards be established before the programme advances.” It, therefore, called on the government to among other things publish the official coordinates, licence instruments, conditions and approved work programmes for all ten offshore reconnaissance licences. It also urged the government to commission and publish an independent spatial overlay showing the licences in relation to the 12 nautical mile IEZ, the Greater Cape Three Points MPA, key fishing grounds, spawning and nursery areas, and other sensitive marine habitats. “Government must also determine transparently whether the existing licences should continue unchanged, be modified to exclude sensitive areas, or be cancelled where applicable legal grounds and evidence warrant such action,” it added.

items.title: INEC to politicians on 2027 polls: Your ambitions not worth blood of Nigerians
items.description: •Vows arrests, sanctions for violence, hate speech, vote-buying •Sets to track illegal campaign spending•As voter register tops 103m, 57,000 new BVAS acquired, PVC collection begins Friday By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA—The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has warned politicians that their ambitions were not worth the blood of Nigerians, vowing arrests, sanctions and prosecution against parties, candidates and agents who resort to violence, hate speech and vote-buying during the 2027 general election. INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan SAN, gave the warning at a strategic workshop for editors, organised by the Nigerian Guild of Editors, NGE, in collaboration with the commission, in Abuja yesterday. “As electioneering intensifies across the country, I must sound a clear note of warning to all political parties, candidates, and campaign managers: INEC will not stand by and allow political competition to devolve into violence, intimidation, or inflammatory rhetoric. “Democracy thrives on the clash of ideas, not the clash of weapons or the proliferation of hate speech,” he stated. Amupitan said the commission had put machinery in place to track offenders, adding that “through the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security, ICCES, we have activated an early-warning tracking framework to log incidents of political violence, thuggery and dangerous campaign rhetoric. “Any political party or candidate implicated in inciting violence, disrupting rivals’ rallies or deploying armed thugs will face direct statutory sanctions and swift prosecution. No political office in this country is worth the blood of a single Nigerian.’’ Departing from his prepared speech, the chairman said he had just been shown evidence of the kind of conduct he was warning against. “Just before I was invited to come and speak, somebody shared with me… a person, an NDC candidate in Kano State who was campaigning yesterday with a gun in his hands, brandishing the gun, and so on and so forth. “Another person was threatening that with AK-47s, they will kill all of us in the commission. So, that is what elections have turned into in Nigeria of today,” Amupitan lamented. He appealed for restraint, saying “let us not forget our role as citizens of Nigeria to be patriotic because election is a periodic process for the election of leaders every four years”. Vote-buying On vote-buying, the chairman also announced a crackdown on money politics, stressing that the integrity of the ballot box was fatally compromised when a citizen’s vote was treated as a commodity for sale. “The commission is taking an uncompromising stance against vote-buying in all its forms ahead of the 2027 general election,” he said. He disclosed that the commission was working with the Federal Ministry of Justice, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission EFCC, the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission, ICPC, and the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit NFIU. 103m registrants On the voter register, Amupitan said Phase I of the Continuous Voter Registration, CVR, which ran from August 25, 2025, to December 10, 2025, registered 2,611,266 voters, while Phase II, from January 5 to April 17, 2026, registered 4,121,835. According to him, Phase III, from May 11 to July 26, 2026, registered 3,867,997, which together amount to over 10.6 million new registrants. 57,000 new BVAS On technology, Amupitan said the commission had acquired 57,000 new Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, devices “for optimal performance.” He said the enhanced eEC8A system digitised polling unit result sheets, authenticated them cryptographically and uploaded them directly from polling units to the INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV. Amupitan said Form eEC8A would halt manipulation of votes at the polling unit level before the figures were entered into the BVAS and transferred to IReV. Bulletproof vests, cars He disclosed that at the commission’s North-West zonal engagement in Kaduna State, staff from Zamfara, Sokoto and other states asked for bulletproof vests and vehicles because of insecurity in parts of those states. He said the commission might secure bulletproof vehicles for staff in flashpoints, noting that the commission had completed physical readiness audits and staff engagements in the South-West and North-West zones, covering state office facilities, safe storage, security command protocols and logistics networks, adding that the other four geopolitical zones would follow. Speaking on the issue of staff welfare, he said the commission had “recently introduced the Consolidated Election Management Body Salary Structure, CEMBSS, accompanied by a 150% increase in state office operational overheads effective July 1, 2026. ‘’We are working on the cash backing to ensure immediate implementation,’’ he added. In his remarks, NGE President, Mr Eze Anaba, said the partnership was timely as the country approached another round of elections. “Elections are not merely about casting ballots; they are about trust. They are about citizens believing that their votes will count, that the process will be transparent and that the institutions responsible for conducting elections will act fairly and professionally,” he said. Anaba said the media had a critical role in building and sustaining that trust, noting that “as editors, we determine, to a significant extent, what information reaches the public, how it is presented and the context in which it is understood. With that responsibility comes an obligation to uphold accuracy, fairness, balance and the public interest,” he said. He acknowledged that the media could carry the responsibility alone. “At the same time, we recognise that the media cannot perform this responsibility effectively without credible, timely and accessible information from the electoral management body,” he said. Anaba, who warned of the environment in which both sides operate, said: “In an environment increasingly polluted by misinformation, disinformation, manipulated content, deepfakes and partisan narratives, the relationship between INEC and the media must therefore be one founded on openness, mutual respect and regular engagement.’’ The post INEC to politicians on 2027 polls: Your ambitions not worth blood of Nigerians appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NYSC kidnap: ‘Bring my son, others back alive,’ mother begs FG
items.description: —Afenifere demand safer deployment By Adeola Badru IBADAN—A 55-year-old mother, Janet Oladosu, has appealed to the Federal Government to intensify efforts to rescue her son, Greatness, and 19 other prospective National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, members abducted while travelling to their orientation camps. Speaking with Vanguard yesterday, Oladosu urged the Federal Government, Oyo and Imo State governments and security agencies to make the rescue of the victims a priority. “All I want is for my son to come back alive. These are young Nigerians who were simply travelling to serve their country,” she said. The 20 prospective corps members, who had collected their NYSC call-up letters, reportedly departed from the Samonda area of Ibadan on September 30, 2026, for orientation camps in the South-East and South-South. They were reportedly abducted near Umunoha in Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State while travelling towards Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, and Bende, Abia State. Oladosu said her son had kept her informed of his movements throughout the journey from Ibadan until a message from him suddenly changed the nature of their communication. According to her, Greatness had earlier told her that a prolonged traffic hold-up in Edo State forced the travellers to stop over in Anambra State because it had become too late to continue the journey. She said he contacted her again the following morning to inform her that they had resumed their journey towards Imo State. “But about 45 minutes later, I received a message from him through another phone. It read: ‘Mummy, we have been kidnapped,’” she said. Oladosu said another message from her son revealed the circumstances under which he contacted her. “He wrote: ‘Mummy, I don’t know what will happen to us. I hid this phone in my trouser to send a text to you,’” she recalled. She said the message heightened her fears because her son was communicating secretly while in captivity and was uncertain about what would happen to him and the other victims. The incident has triggered renewed calls for a review of the NYSC deployment policy, with the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, calling for reforms to reduce the security risks faced by prospective corps members travelling long distances for national service. In a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Jare Ajayi, yesterday, Afenifere urged the Federal Government to expedite amendment of the NYSC Act to allow graduates serve in their states of origin, states of residence or, at least, within their geopolitical zones. Ajayi said Afenifere had consistently advocated a review of the deployment policy since 2021, particularly following incidents involving the kidnapping or attack of corps members. According to him, the objective was to reduce the need for prospective corps members to travel from one part of the country to another to undertake national service. Afenifere also urged the Federal Government, security agencies and the Oyo and Imo State governments to intensify efforts to rescue the abducted graduates. The group recalled President Bola Tinubu’s July announcement that the Federal Ministries of Youth Development and Justice had been directed to commence the process of amending the NYSC Act and its subsidiary regulations to give legal backing to reforms approved by the Federal Executive Council. The proposed reforms include risk-based deployment, particularly in states facing security challenges. Afenifere urged the government to accelerate the legislative process and ensure that the proposed reforms translate into concrete measures to protect corps members. Pending the amendment, the group called on the NYSC to allow graduates to serve in their states of origin, states of residence or neighbouring states within their geopolitical zones. It also commended President Tinubu for approving additional Army formations in Zamfara, Kebbi, Oyo and Osun states, saying the development would bring troops closer to vulnerable communities and improve response to security emergencies. However, Afenifere said military expansion alone would not end kidnapping and banditry, urging effective enforcement of the 2022 Terrorism (Prevention and Prohibition) Act. items.title: Gov’t is committed to addressing teachers’ conditions of service, deprived-area allowance – Minister
items.description: Haruna Iddrisu, the Minister of Education, on Monday reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to resolving outstanding grievances of teachers, including the payment of promotion arrears and the implementation of the deprived-area allowance. He noted that the Government had initiated processes to address the concerns raised by the teacher unions and improve conditions of service in the education sector. Mr Iddrisu gave the assurance at this year’s Ghana Teacher Prize to commemorate teachers and recognise their contribution to national development. He said the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission, with the support of the Ministry of Finance, would engage the teacher unions on their expired collective agreement on conditions of service. He said the Government was committed to fulfilling its manifesto pledge on the payment of a deprived-area allowance to teachers serving in underserved communities. The education minister said discussions were ongoing to validate the data on deprived schools and communities to determine who qualified for the allowance and ensure its effective implementation. “We are sure that there is absolute government commitment to the manifesto pledge on the deprived-area allowance. What we need to do is validate the data, then we can begin the process of implementation,” he said. The Minister said the Government had also committed resources to clear outstanding promotion arrears to teachers. The Ghana Education Service, in collaboration with the relevant institutions, had been tasked to validate the records of teachers who had been promoted but were yet to receive their new salary grades and associated arrears, he explained. Mr Iddrisu said the exercise was expected to cover more than 51,000 teachers, adding that the Government would make the necessary financial arrangements to settle the outstanding arrears. The minister commended teachers for their contribution to the development of the country, describing them as the “architects” of every profession. “We all owe it to the teacher. No profession is possible without the teacher, and for that reason, we recognise you and celebrate you,” he said. The education minister disclosed that President John Dramani Mahama had approved a new integrated model for basic education infrastructure. He said the model would bring key basic education facilities together within a single development to ensure more efficient use of resources and improve access to quality education. Under the proposed model, a basic school complex would include kindergarten, primary and junior high school facilities, as well as laboratories, libraries and information technology facilities. He said the Government had directed Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies to ensure that new basic education infrastructure reflected the integrated model. Mr Iddrisu said the initiative was part of efforts to address infrastructure deficits in the education sector, particularly the large number of schools without electricity. He cited data indicating that about 10,750 schools across the country were still without electricity, affecting approximately three million children. He said the government would work to mobilise resources through the appropriate funding mechanisms to reduce the infrastructure deficit and ensure that pupils and teachers had access to better learning environments. Mr Prosper Tachie, the President, Ghana National Association of Teachers,called for the empowerment of teachers in three key areas; legal authority, professional confidence, and economic security. He said teachers needed the legal authority to perform their professional responsibilities, including maintaining discipline in schools, while also having the confidence and financial security to meet their basic needs. He cited a World Bank report on the global teaching profession published in May 2026, which emphasised the importance of teachers to the skills development of the global workforce. Mr Tachie called for greater involvement of teachers in education policy formulation, saying their experiences at the classroom level should inform decisions affecting the sector.

items.title: Les grands laboratoires pharmaceutiques se tournent vers les biotechs chinoises
items.description: D'ici la fin de la décennie, de médicaments des marques, représentant plus de 200 milliards de dollars de ventes pourraient perdre la protection de leurs brevets. Pour renouveler leurs portefeuilles, les grands laboratoires se tournent de plus en plus vers les biotechs chinoises, dont ils acquièrent les licences des futurs médicaments The world is flat for pharma, until it isn’t , Global Trade Policy Observatory (GTPO), 10 septembre 2026.'> 1 . Selon Tim Opler, directeur du Global Healthcare Group de la banque d'investissement Stifel, les médicaments chinois représentent cette année plus de la moitié des sommes engagées par les grands laboratoires dans des accords de licence. Selon PharmCube, la valeur annoncée des accords conclus par des entreprises chinoises avec des partenaires étrangers a atteint environ 136 milliards de dollars l'an dernier, plus du double du montant de 2024. La taille moyenne des contrats a fortement augmenté depuis 2021, signe d’une montée en gamme des actifs chinois. Ces montants incluent toutefois des paiements conditionnels, versés uniquement si les candidats-médicaments franchissent certaines étapes. La tendance n'en est pas moins nette : selon Locust Walk, les vendeurs chinois ont capté près de la moitié de la valeur des accords de licence pharmaceutiques l'an dernier. La part des actifs d'origine chinoise dans les portefeuilles des grands laboratoires reste limitée (environ 8 % chez les plus exposés), mais cet indicateur ne reflète qu'avec retard l'accélération récente des transactions. En Chine, le nombre de candidats-médicaments a augmenté de 36 % en un an, portant le total à 7 105. Les États-Unis restent largement en tête, avec 12 800 candidats-médicaments, mais ce chiffre n'a progressé que de 0,6 % l’an dernier. La Chine mène plus d'essais cliniques de phase précoce que n’importe quelle autre région. Selon la Fédération européenne des industries et associations pharmaceutiques, sur les 104 nouvelles substances actives lancées pour la première fois sur le marché mondial l'an dernier, 46 provenaient d'entreprises chinoises, contre 28 d'entreprises américaines et 16 d'entreprises européennes. La Chine offre aux laboratoires une exécution plus rapide et moins coûteuse qu'en Occident, ainsi que la capacité de monter rapidement en puissance.. Cette année, Pékin a classé la biomédecine parmi les « secteurs clefs en développement », et le 15e plan quinquennal (2026-2030) fait de la biofabrication une industrie d'avenir. Plus largement, la Chine a lancé en décembre un fonds national de capital-risque de 100 milliards de yuans (13,3 milliards d'euros), consacré aux technologies de pointe, dont la biofabrication. Il doit à terme mobiliser 1 000 milliards de yuans de financements régionaux et privés. Au moins 70 % de ces fonds iront à des entreprises en phase d'amorçage ou de démarrage. Les laboratoires occidentaux conservent pour l’heure une avance dans les médicaments dits « first-in-class », mais cet écart pourrait se réduire. Les biotechs chinoises se distinguent surtout par leur production rapide de candidats-médicaments, leur recherche précoce et leurs coûts réduits. De leur côté, les laboratoires occidentaux continueraient de dominer les activités qui concentrent la majeure partie de la valeur, comme le développement clinique avancé, les relations avec les régulateurs et les payeurs, la production mondiale et la commercialisation. L'essor de la Chine pourrait alors déboucher sur une division du travail profitable aux deux parties. Mais si l'écosystème chinois s’impose comme le lieu le plus efficace pour la recherche rapide, la production de données et la création de nouveaux principes actifs, les grands laboratoires pourraient finir par dépendre de plus en plus d’acteurs chinois, même s’ils gardent le contrôle de la commercialisation. La Chine a déjà acquis une expertise de pointe dans certaines technologies, comme les anticorps conjugués ou les thérapies CAR-T. Or, cet écosystème reste dépendant de l'État, qui peut intervenir sur les flux de données, les licences d'exportation, les investissements ou les transferts de technologie. Aux États-Unis, cette question fait l'objet de discussions entre responsables politiques et représentants de l’industrie. La Commission des crédits de la Chambre des représentants a ainsi approuvé un rapport non contraignant qui propose d’interdire à la FDA, l’agence chargée de protéger la santé publique, de prendre en compte les données cliniques obtenues en Chine, en Russie, en Iran ou en Corée du Nord dans les demandes d’autorisation pour certains essais cliniques. La proposition de loi BINSA déposée en juin à la Chambre et en août au Sénat prévoit d’étendre à la biotechnologie le contrôle américain des investissements réalisés à l’étranger. Elle modifierait la loi COINS, adoptée dans le cadre du National Defense Authorization Act de 2026, la loi annuelle qui fixe les dépenses de défense. Le Trésor américain est tenu de publier les règlements d’application d’ici mars 2027. L’Europe, quant à elle, dispose d’une base scientifique importante, et ses chercheurs sont à l’origine de plus d’un cinquième des publications de référence dans le domaine de la biotechnologie (21 %) – soit une part comparable à celle des États-Unis et de la Chine. L’article Les grands laboratoires pharmaceutiques se tournent vers les biotechs chinoises est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Traffic, not sour grapes, kept Nana Akomea away from NPP swearing-in
items.description: Newly elected NPP Third Vice Chairperson Nana Akomea has dismissed suggestions that he boycotted the party’s swearing-in ceremony after finishing third in the vice-chairmanship contest. He says traffic delayed his arrival at the venue. Nana Akomea explained that he reached the stadium about 10 minutes after the swearing-in had already taken place. “They had just introduced the witness and done the swearing. Actually, when we entered the stadium, we heard because we could hear to the radio that the swearing was going on.” He said he was not at the venue when voting, collation and counting were completed. “So I wasn’t even there when the voting finished, and for the collation and the counting, for me to go and even speak to anybody.” Akomea said his agents were present and informed him of the outcome. “Oh, my agents were there, and then when I got there, the swearing had been done. So I knew I had taken the third position, and I was rushing to go for the swearing-in.” He also said Nana B, another candidate in the contest, was similarly delayed. “I don’t know. I think Nana B was caught up in the same traffic.” Akomea rejected suggestions that his absence was linked to disappointment over Kojo Bamba’s victory. “I got there 10 minutes after the swearing in.” He confirmed that he was at the stadium after the ceremony but had not been sworn in. “Yeah.” He said he expected to be sworn in at a subsequent meeting of the new national executive. “Well, remember there’s an American president who had to be sworn in twice, so that is not new. We have our first meeting as a new executive, and I’m sure I’ll get myself sworn in.” Akomea also dismissed the suggestion that his absence, alongside Nana B’s, could be interpreted as sour grapes. “because of the coincidence. Because both of us were, but we’re not there. Nana B said he fell into traffic coming to the place.” He said he had been disappointed by the election result but maintained that his campaign message had been well received. “Yeah.” “Oh, because, as I said, my message was well received.” Akomea said he had expected to finish higher in the contest. “Yes, even though I had come in late, many of the delegates expressed disappointment that I had come in late.” He also acknowledged that campaign spending could have influenced the outcome. “But I came in when the nominations opened, so the fact that somebody came before me was that you were outspent. Let’s be honest about that. Were you outspent? It’s possible, and it’s also possible that I also outspent somebody.”

items.title: Pims gets new executive director and joint executive director, notifications raise eyebrows
items.description: ISLAMABAD: After almost six weeks having passed since the fire incident , the capital’s largest hospital Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) got a new executive director (ED) and joint executive director (JED). However, the notifications raised eye brows as the charge of ED has been given to an officer who has passed his age of superannuation while the JED’s charge has been given to a contractual employee who has been working in the hospital for the last over one year. It is worth mentioning here that after the fire incident at Pims in which 14 newborn babies had died on August 26 and later the 15th baby also passed away , Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had taken notice and suspended as many as eight officers. The charge of ED was given to Dr Mohammad Salman who is also head of the National Institute of Health (NIH). According to two notifications, available with Dawn , in pursuance of the directives of the Prime Minister’s Office, Prof Dr Tanwir Khaliq currently posted as vice chancellor, Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University (SZABMU), Islamabad has been assigned the additional charge of the post of executive director (BPS-21), Pims, in addition to his own duties for a period of three months or till the availability of regular incumbent of the post, whichever is earlier. “The officer will be entitled to draw additional remuneration as admissible under the rules. Dr. Mohammad Salman presently working as executive director (BPS-21), Pims, Islamabad is hereby repatriated to his parent department and directed to resume his duties on same positions in NIH, Islamabad with immediate effect,” the notification reads. The second notification states: “With the approval of the competent authority i.e. Secretary, Ministry of Health, Prof. Dr. Brig. (Retd.) Azmat Hayat, Professor of Electrophysiology, Pims, Islamabad is hereby assigned additional charge of the post of Joint Executive Director (BPS-20/Medical), Pims, in addition to his own duties for a period of three months or till the availability of regular incumbent of the post, whichever is earlier. The officer will be entitled to draw additional remuneration as admissible under the rules.” A senior doctor of the hospital, wishing not to be named, said Dr Tanwir Khaliq had retired almost six years ago. “Now additional charge of the hospital head has been given to him. We (doctors) cannot understand that how he will handle two jobs,” he asked. “Prof. Dr. Brig. (Retd.) Azmat Hayat was working in Pims as a contractual employee in MP-II scale. Now he has got the position of JED in the hospital. I don’t remember if a contractual employee got such position in the past,” he said. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

Gaza: le chef de l'ONU demande un cessez-le-feu permanent
items.description: Le secrétaire général des Nations unies a plaidé lundi en faveur d'un « cessez-le-feu permanent » à Gaza entre Israël et le Hamas, à l'avant-veille du troisième anniversaire de l'attaque du 7 octobre 2023. « Il est temps que le cessez-le-feu devienne permanent. Il est temps de permettre une aide humanitaire à grande échelle. Et il est temps de respecter le droit international », a déclaré Antonio Guterres dans un communiqué. « Nous devons construire une voie politique vers une paix durable dans toute la région. Les Nations unies restent inébranlables dans leur engagement envers ces impératifs », a-t-il poursuivi. M. Guterres a aussi appelé à bâtir « un avenir dans lequel Israéliens et Palestiniens pourront vivre côte à côte dans la paix et la sécurité, avec leurs droits, leur dignité et leurs aspirations pleinement réalisés. » Les attaques commises par le Hamas sur le sol israélien le 7 octobre 2023, qualifiées d' »abjectes » par le chef de l'ONU, ont entraîné la mort de 1.221 personnes du côté israélien, en majorité des civils, selon un décompte de l'AFP basé sur des données officielles. « Je pleure ceux qui ont été tués lors des attaques et ceux qui sont morts en captivité. Leurs souffrances, et le deuil sans fin de leurs familles, ne doivent jamais être oubliés », écrit M. Guterres. L'offensive lancée en représailles par Israël à Gaza a fait plus de 74.200 morts, selon le ministère de la Santé du territoire palestinien, placé sous l'autorité du Hamas et dont les chiffres sont jugés fiables par l'ONU. Dans l'enclave palestinienne, « les civils continuent d'endurer des conditions intolérables. Leur souffrance, elle aussi, exige qu'on y mette fin, maintenant », ajoute Antonio Guterres. Depuis le cessez-le-feu annoncé par le président américain, Donald Trump, en octobre 2025, l'avenir politique du territoire demeure incertain. Israël, qui contrôle toujours la majeure partie de Gaza, refuse d'en retirer ses forces tant que le désarmement du Hamas n'aura pas été vérifié. Le Hamas défend de son côté un désarmement progressif, plutôt qu'une reddition immédiate et unilatérale de son arsenal. Dans le sillage de l'attaque du Hamas, Israël a combattu sur plusieurs fronts, notamment au Liban face au Hezbollah, mouvement islamiste soutenu par Téhéran, ainsi que contre l'Iran. items.title: Mental health: Psychiatrist to highlight tech-based treatment at Vanguard summit
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe Young Nigerians battling mental health conditions, such as depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, OCD, and post-traumatic stress disorder, PTSD, who fail to respond to conventional treatment could have another treatment option known as Transcranial Magnetic Stimulatio, TMS, as an additional pathway for managing the conditions. Dr Olufemi Oluwatayo, a Consultant Psychiatrist, Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, London, and Medical Director, Ikeja Specialist Clinic & TMS Centre, Lagos, will speak on TMS at the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit, which opens Friday, October 9, 2026, at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Oluwatayo’s presentation will form part of the broader discussion at the summit on the place of technology in youth mental health, examining not only the challenges technology can create but also how it may expand treatment options for young people. The summit is themed “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria through Access, Action and Advocacy,” with the sub-theme “Mental Health in a Digital Age: Navigating Social Media, Technology and Wellbeing.” In his presentation, titled “Using Technology to Manage Common Mental Health Conditions in Youths: The Role of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Treatment,” Oluwatayo who also the Chief Executive Officer of Retreat Healthcare, Ikorodu, will examine how TMS can be used in managing depression, anxiety, OCD and PTSD, particularly where conventional approaches have not produced the desired response. “Depression, anxiety, Obsessive Compulsive disorders and PTSD are common in young people and often go unrecognised. They may not respond to the usual first line treatments, i.e. antidepressants and talking therapy. Also, common antidepressants often present with side-effects, and adherence is poor. For these reasons, TMS should be considered as a treatment option,” he argued. According to the specialist, young people are technology savvy and are more receptive to technology-based treatment. “Research has shown that it is safe for use in young people just as in adults as it has no lasting side effects,” he said. TMS is a non-invasive treatment that uses magnetic pulses to stimulate specific areas of the brain. Explaining how it works, Oluwatayo said: “A TMS machine produces pulses that are passed through magnetic coils to generate magnetic waves. The magnetic coils are placed on specific parts of the scalp on the head to target certain parts of the brain. “The waves from the coils induce tiny electric currents in the part of the brain that is targeted. This resets dysfunctional brain patterns associated with those conditions.” Further, he said the treatment is tailored to the condition being treated. “The part of the brain targeted depends on the condition being treated. The intensity of the waves and the duration of treatment also depends on the condition. Over the past 10 years or so different centres in the US, UK and Australia have developed different protocols for different conditions,” he said. He identified two common TMS protocols are the standard type and the accelerated type. “In the standard protocol, a session lasts for 30 minutes and is given five days a week for six weeks. Whilst the accelerated protocol lasts for only a few minutes and is repeated several times a day over a two weeks period. “The overall number of treatments for both protocols is 30 but given over a shorter period in the accelerated protocol,” he added. On treatment outcomes, Oluwatayo said: “There are research and clinical evidence that it works in 50 percent of patients who have failed to respond to other treatments. It is well tolerated with only brief scalp aches and tiredness after the treatments, the common side effects.” Although there will be no live demonstration at the summit, participants will see a video explaining how the treatment is administered. “It is impossible to do a real life demonstration but I will show a video of how it is used and pictures of the machine at the clinic,” Oluwatayo said. TMS is available at the Ikeja clinic, which has partnered with a UK company for training and technical support. items.title: Middle class by habit
items.description: IT may not be inaccurate to say that Manmohan Singh created India’s middle class, and the middle class created Narendra Modi. Marxists call them/us the ‘vacillating class’. Janus-like, we are suspiciously double-faced and have a split identity. We look towards the capitalists with one face, wishing to join their ranks and protect property rights. And we look towards the working class with the other face, sharing their economic anxiety and fear of being ruined by big corporations. Given that powerful protests have mushroomed since July across India, mostly led by young students and unemployed youth, it could be signalling a significant disenchantment with the system that has wooed middle class support since 1991. Before Manmohan Singh’s economic reforms as finance minister and his subsequent decade as prime minister (2004-2014), India’s middle class was miniscule, estimated at roughly 2.5 million people earning over $10,000 annually or representing a small, state-controlled bureaucratic and managerial stratum. Following the 1991 liberalisation and the growth of the IT, services, and corporate sectors, the middle class expanded dramatically. By 2015, the number of Indians earning over $10,000 annually grew to 55m. Other estimates placed the middle class at roughly 142m people (about 12 per cent of the population) by the early 2010s, when they were entering various tiers of the middle or ‘neo-middle’ class depending on purchasing power parity of around $10-$50 per day. After Singh left office in 2014, the expansion plateaued for many households due to rising living costs, stagnant real wages, and a K-shaped economic recovery, where wealth concentrated more heavily at the very top. The Modi-led alliance of big business and right-wing street thugs peaked during the Covid-19 episode when the government asked the people to bang their pots and pans to drive away the virus and the UN secretary-general warned that liberalising the exploitation of coal, which the government had announced bang in the middle of the crisis, was hardly the prescribed method to fight the deadly scourge sweeping India and the rest of the world. The young protesters may have to engage with the fact that India’s growth has been consumer-led and K-shaped, with deepening inequality. An Oxfam report in November 2021 said Indian billionaires increased their wealth by 35pc during the lockdown to three trillion, ranking India after the US, China, Germany, Russia, and France. Out of these, the rise in fortunes for the top 100 billionaires since the lockdown was estimated as enough to give every one of the 138m poorest Indian people a cheque for Indian rupees 94,045 each. Oxfam’s Inequality Virus Report was released at the remotely conducted World Economic Forum in Davos. Should it interest the protesters that the wealth of just the top 11 billionaires during the pandemic could easily sustain the MGNREGS — the 2005 social welfare law guaranteeing rural employment — or the health ministry for the next 10 years? Instead, inequalities deepened during Covid-19 when the wealthiest escaped the worst impact of the pandemic and the poor faced joblessness, starvation, and death. A tycoon who emerged as the richest man in India and Asia, earned INR900m an hour during the pandemic when around 24pc of the people in the country were earning under INR3,000 a month during the lockdown. A reintroduction of the wealth tax was advised as a one-time Covid-19 cess of 4pc on taxable income of over a million Indian rupees to help the economy recover from the lockdown. The rejected tax on the nation’s 954 richest families could have raised the equivalent of 1pc of GDP. Even as they seek to repair India’s broken democracy, which is a most crucial task, the young protesters may have to engage with the fact that India’s growth has been consumer-led and K-shaped, with deepening inequality. In comparison, China’s modern economic growth model has been state-led, investment-heavy, and steered by a policy of ‘common prosperity’. India’s middle classes must relearn that China’s current economic strategy shares striking structural DNA with Jawaharlal Nehru’s original vision for India, albeit with a divergence in political execution. Both models share the foundational belief that a post-colonial nation cannot rely on the unbridled free market to achieve greatness or equity. Ergo, the state must control the ‘commanding heights’ of the economy to guide development. Nehru, reviled by the Modi echo chamber, famously insisted that the state must control the core sectors of the economy (steel, power, heavy machinery, and infrastructure) through public sector undertakings. China achieved this exact goal through its massive state-owned enterprises and state-run banks, ensuring that private billionaires never overpower the national agenda. Singh swore by Nehru but failed to appreciate that Nehru was deeply wary of the concentration of private wealth, fearing it would corrupt society and exploit the poor. China’s common prosperity drive — manifested in aggressive regulatory crackdowns on tech monopolies, tutoring companies, and real estate moguls — is driven by the same suspicion of oligarchic power. Nehru viewed heavy industries as the “temples of modern India”. Beijing’s pursuit of “new productive forces” (semiconductors, green energy, EVs, and AI) represents a modern, high-tech version of Nehruvian import-substitution and state-directed scientific self-reliance. Unlike Singh’s rely-on-services trajectory, China historically built a manufacturing-and-export juggernaut, which is currently transitioning into a paradigm-focused, state-mandated wealth redistribution. Indira Gandhi nationalised banks to pursue an equitable Nehruvian agenda to serve the masses. Singh, however, set the stage for opening the backdoor of state-owned banks to private plunderers that Modi turned into an art. Singh saw Babri Masjid’s destruction as finance minister but concluded that the biggest internal threat to India came from Maoist tribespeople, exactly the opposite of Nehru’s assessment that it was the right-wing Hindu movement that posed a mortal challenge to Indian democracy, not communists. Would the protesters, overwhelmingly from the middle classes, heed the discussion — but only after winning their battle against the current right-wing government — and ask why 800m compatriots remain on food dole in one of the world’s largest economies built by Manmohan Singh? The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi. jawednaqvi@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

items.title: Trump says he will stop using taxpayer funds for ads after bipartisan pushback
items.description: President Donald Trump has said he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television ads he has fronted, following bipartisan pushback. “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” he said Monday on social media. Trump said it is “a rather standard thing to do” but that he has decided to pay for the “Patriotic Ads” himself and with money he raised through his MAGA Inc super political action committee. The ads, which praise the president and his policies, drew criticism and questions about their legality under laws against using government money for political ads. There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning Trump’s tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the “deep state” and others he perceives as enemies. In one ad, Trump says, “We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all”. The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections , when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump’s approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing – and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress. The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads “educational” and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements. They’ve pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines. But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies. “It’s difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president,” legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC. Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads. “It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language ‘paid for by the U.S. Government,’ should not be paid for by the United States government,” the measure reads. The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle. Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while “I like the message … it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”. Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads. “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves,” the Louisiana lawmaker said.

items.title: Ex-NADECO founding member, Ralph Obioha, dies at 80
items.description: A founding member of the National Democratic Coalition, NADECO, Chief Ralph Obioha is dead, aged 80. In a statement by his son, Chima Obioha on behalf of the Obioha family in Enugu, said: “It is with profound sadness and heavy hearts that the family of Chief Ralph Obioha, “Okpuruisizuruoha II of Arondizuogu announces his passing on October 3, 2026, at the age of 80. Chief Obioha was first and foremost a beloved father, husband, brother, grandfather and friend. His kindness, strength, humor, generosity, faith, and unwavering devotion to family will always be r ememb e r e d . “Many Nigerians knew Chief Obioha as a patriot, elder statesman, political leader and businessman. Indeed, his very eventful life spanned various business sectors and the Nigerian political and socio- economic space. “He was deeply committed to Nigeria’s progress and the ideals of service, leadership, and nation-building. His was a respected voice in the land, and he was a firm believer in Nigeria’s enormous potential. “His passing has left an immeasurable void in our family, but we find comfort in the fullness of his life, the people he touched, and the legacy of service he leaves behind. “The family is deeply grateful for the prayers, condolence messages, and expressions of love that have already been received. We, however, respectfully request privacy at this time while we mourn and come to terms with this profound loss. “Details of the memorial and funeral will be announced in due course. May his soul rest in complete peace.” the statement added. The post Ex-NADECO founding member, Ralph Obioha, dies at 80 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tunisia: Power, Water Shortages Endanger Rights
items.description: Click to expand Image Cars pass through a darkened street during a nighttime power outage in Ariana, Tunisia, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via AP Photo (Beirut) – Tunisian authorities failed to ensure an adequate supply of electricity and water during two months of extreme summer heat, undermining the right to health and endangering lives, Human Rights Watch said today. President Kais Saied blamed the shortages on sabotage, yet authorities failed to provide transparent information and instead cracked down on protesters. Rolling power outages left hospitals and water pumping stations without electricity and households without running water, interrupted critical medical procedures, and contributed to a nationwide shortage of drinking water. Doctors and human rights groups have reported a rise in heat-related hospitalizations and deaths exacerbated by the cuts, including among detainees. “Tunisians have spent one of the hottest summers on record in the dark and facing water shortages because President Saied’s government failed to ensure adequate access to electricity for millions of people, risking lives,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “Instead of blaming sabotage, the authorities should address the root causes of the failure and ensure that everyone, including detainees, has access to water, electricity, and methods for cooling.” In July 2026, the second-hottest July since 1950, the Tunisian Electricity and Gas Company (STEG) reportedly imposed rotating outages due to inadequate capacity. Power outages were concentrated between 1 and 5 p.m., when air conditioning increased demand. According to crowd-sourced data, outages lasted up to 12 hours in some extreme cases. In late August, a second wave led to cuts of up to two hours at a time in every region. Tunisian authorities have not published transparent information about the impact of the outages. The Tunisian Young Doctors Association estimated on July 22 that between 150 and 200 people had died over the previous days from heatstroke or medical equipment failure in the case of patients who depended on electrically powered medical equipment. It reported on August 28 that emergency departments experienced an “unprecedented” rise in deaths and hospitalizations from heatstroke and high temperatures, including deaths of detainees. Local media reported five deaths after respirators in the victims’ homes stopped working. Four parliament members wrote to the health minister on July 23 about patients on home oxygen therapy. The Health Ministry on August 29 reported 633 medical cases related to the heat wave in public hospitals but made no mention of related deaths. The ministry also denied that health services had been disrupted. A doctor at one of Tunis’s largest hospitals told Human Rights Watch that due to limited generator capacity, the outages meant the hospital went without electricity in most areas. Its backup generator covered only the intensive care units and operating rooms, the doctor said, while the rest of the building, including the emergency department, had no backup power or contingency plan. Because hospital admissions depended on electronic medical records, staff could not register patients arriving during an outage, even those with life-threatening conditions. During one outage, neonatal unit doctors ventilated newborns by hand. Outages also affected recovery for patients in post-operative care left without ventilation or air conditioning, the doctor said. The blackouts also disrupted the water supply. As outages disrupted pumping stations, tap water became intermittent in many parts of Tunisia. The Tunisian Water Observatory recorded 361 cuts to distribution of potable water in August, contributing to a bottled water shortage in a country where much of the population relies on it as their main drinking source. Although the National Authority for Food Safety said tap water is safe, public confidence is low, with reports of cloudy or yellowed water and changes in taste and odor. Water and electricity cuts affected prisons and detention sites. On August 28, five detainees at Mornaguia prison reportedly died in one day. The Tunisian League for Human Rights documented 20 deaths in prisons and detention facilities amid conditions exacerbated by extreme heat and water and power outages. The General Secretary of the General Federation of Electricity and Gas said that STEG had alerted its supervising ministry to the risk of power shortfalls and need for additional capacity as early as 2024. A 2026 report by the Tunisian Economy Observatory found that STEG's investment in generating electricity fell by 87 percent over five years. Tunisian authorities provided no evidence of sabotage. In late July, prosecutors’ offices across the country opened investigations into STEG managers and employees. President Saied said on August 26 that the outages in several regions were not “ordinary outages,” but rather “deliberately planned acts of sabotage” intended to stoke tensions, spread lies and rumors, and deprive citizens of their right to access services, but provided no further information. The electricity crisis was foreseeable, and Tunisian authorities had an obligation to prepare for it, including by ensuring that essential services such as water supply and health care were not affected, Human Rights Watch said. The government’s mismanagement and failure to act preemptively compounded the harm. Protests over water and electricity shortages have spread. The Tunisian Social Observatory of the Tunisian Forum for Economic and Social Rights recorded 1,101 protest actions in July and 1,093 in August in all 24 governorates, the highest July and August figures in years. Following an August 13 protest in Borj Erras over the lack of water, the authorities arrested 12 people, including 9 children, investigating them on suspicion of conspiring against state security, then releasing them the next day. On August 20, the grassroots movement Nafas held a demonstration in Tunis under the slogan “No water, no electricity, no freedom.” The next day, the authorities arrested Seifeddine Arfaoui, a political activist and Nafas member, at his home. On August 31, a Tunis court sentenced him to 18 months in prison under article 86 of the Telecommunications Code, for a Facebook post about slogans chanted at the protest. Human Rights Watch has previously documented a years-long crackdown against all forms of dissent in Tunisia. Access to electricity is critical to ensuring other rights, including but not limited to health, housing, water, and education, and should be recognized as a distinct human right, Human Rights Watch said. Tunisia has an obligation to ensure access to electricity and water, including within prisons and detention facilities. Article 48 of the Tunisian Constitution requires the state to provide drinking water to everyone on an equal basis. The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights guarantees the right to an adequate standard of living and the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights has held that a government's failure to provide basic services including safe drinking water and electricity violates the right to health under the African Charter. As a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the African Charter, Tunisia is also bound to respect the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. “Tunisian authorities have known for years that the electricity grid was inadequate but failed to plan for rising demand and the risks of a scorching summer,” Khawaja said. “Instead of prosecuting protesters, the government should publicly account for the failures of the electric grid, publicize transparent information including a death toll, and set out a clear plan to restore adequate electricity and water.”

items.title: Naira rises to N1,357/$ in parallel market
items.description: By Elizabeth Adegbesan The Naira yesterday appreciated to N1,357 per dollar from N1,362 in the parallel market last weekend. But the naira depreciated to N1,332.9 per dollar in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, NFEM. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, showed that the indicative exchange rate for the naira rose to N1,332.9 per dollar from N1,332 per dollar last weekend, indicating 90 kobo depreciation for the naira. Consequently, the margin between the parallel and official markets narrowed to N24.1 per dollar from N30 per dollar last weekend. The value of interbank turnover in NFEM fell by 66 percent to $72.12 million from $154.02 million last weekend. The post Naira rises to N1,357/$ in parallel market appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Magical confusion
items.description: LAST night, I dreamt of Hogwarts again. Indeed, the time is ripe to revisit Harry Potter and Hogwarts — the boarding school where the series is based — for here in Pakistan, we are living in the most ‘confunding’ times possible. Surely, the ‘Confundus Charm’ has been used on everyone. And the result is greater confusion than ever before. Let us begin at the beginning. Of late, the soothsayers among our midst, like Prof Trelawny, have rarely got a prophecy right. For days, they told us ominously that decisions had been made. First came the warning about the departure of Sohail Afridi. Within days, we were forewarned. And then the tea leaves predicted an emergency in KP. Apparently, it was the only province with a dysfunctional government — the rest are all on their way to winning the Triwizard Cup. But these leaf readers do not face consequences. Indeed, they were hardly employed for their competence. For a number of them, the job has not been to report, analyse, or communicate. Instead, comfortably employed, they do what a ‘howler’ does in the Harry Potter series — pass messages to those who have fallen into disfavour, before ‘self-destructing’ once the job is done. Dignity and credibility appear to have little to do with messaging — neither for these ‘journalists’ nor the politicos who tweet similar warnings. Be that as it may, the problem lies less with the messengers and more with the higher-ups guiding them, and who tell them to announce a disqualification one day and an emergency the next. And then opt for talks, which clearly were not going to succeed — because neither side wanted to negotiate. They simply wanted to win. Pakistan’s current political landscape bears a striking resemblance to the world of Harry Potter. Consider that for weeks, the PTI was pushing for access to Imran Khan and treatment for his health issues but by the time the talks were held, the focus shifted to terrorism. The government had spent most of its energies on explaining how the party’s founding chairman was fine and was receiving the medical treatment he needed, and the PTI was just kicking up a fuss for nothing. And then it all shifted. Terrorism entered the conversation as abruptly as the short-lived romance between Hermione and the character called Krum in the fourth Harry Potter book. But while the romance twist was undeveloped, the same cannot be said of the terrorism angle in our politics. Terrorism and its causes have been discussed for very long. But it seems the root of the matter remains unclear to those in power. For longer than can be remembered, the state’s entire focus has been on pushing the idea that terrorism in Pakistan is due to the foreign hand. The groups carrying out attacks are called Fitna al-Hindustan and Fitna al-Khawarij. When attacks take place in Pakistan, it puts pressure on the relationship with Kabul as usually the attacker’s identity is linked to the lands across the border, also referred to as the ‘Durand Line’. Operations are carried out and these slow down the pace of attacks. It was all to do with the external enemies. Suddenly, it turns out that terrorism is due to the uncooperative attitude of the PTI government in Peshawar. This hits as hard as the unexpected death of Sirius Black in the Potter series. Who does one blame now for the attacks? The PTI or the Afghan Taliban? More confusion. It will get worse, I fear, as the talk of emergency and disqualification is back. More howling shall now commence. None of this is to suggest that the other side, the PTI, is the hero here. It is about as self-pitying and as tolerable as Kreacher the elf. The party announced the ‘long march’ without any strategy or plan; it didn’t even consult its allies such as the TTAP. Frankly speaking, all it wanted to do was escape the growing anger of its supporters. And once the announcement was made, then the party leadership (if it can be called that) sat down to figure out a plan. The solution it found was to hope for talks and a negotiated end, allowing it to cancel the march. And that didn’t really work out the way it had hoped, did it? Just like Voldemort’s idea of killing Harry Potter the baby. So now the party is in even more trouble than before. For the establishment is angrier than before and there is little indication the supporters will be satisfied. Quite the dilemma it is; just like Wormtail who tried to play it safe but eventually joined the ‘dark side’, only to end up dead. In comparison, the PPP does seem to have played it well. For the party has perfected the art of changing sides and positions so frequently that it is hard to figure out where it stands at all. Does it even stand? It supports the government, but sits on talk shows and transforms into Moaning Myrtle. And has been doing so for over two years now. Its sources kept telling everyone it would be averse to an emergency and confrontations but came out of the recent PTI-government talks, declaiming its concern and firm stand on terrorism. As if the party is known for its belief in anything but the ‘shyshtem’ in Sindh. And once Mohsin Naqvi (in the manner of Dolores Umbridge, who looked cute and cuddly, but was a hawk) landed in KP, the PPP governor had no qualms about holding a meeting with him along with provincial government officers. Indeed, the PPP, Severus Snape-like, is hard to like and hard to qualify as a good guy. Only death was able to absolve him. With PPP it might just be when it’s out of power — if ever. Postscript: This piece might be of interest only to those who still remember the Harry Potter series. For the rest, there are always the howlers and their predictions. The writer is a journalist. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

items.title: Nana Akomea explains why he ignored polls ahead of NPP election
items.description: Newly elected NPP Third Vice Chairperson Nana Akomea says he paid little attention to opinion polls ahead of the party’s national executive elections. He said direct engagement with delegates gave candidates a better opportunity to assess their chances. “So I didn’t pay much heed to the polls because you are meeting the electorate directly.” Nana Akomea said the NPP election was different from a national election, in which candidates cannot personally engage millions of voters. “This is not a national election of about 14, 15 million people, which you cannot meet directly, except maybe through mass media, social media, and so on.” He said candidates were able to meet delegates directly in relatively small groups and assess their reactions to their messages. “This one, you are meeting the delegates directly. Each constituency had about 19. When you are meeting five constituencies or six cons, you are looking at about 70, 80, 90 people, and so you are meeting them directly, eyeball to eyeball.” Akomea also cautioned candidates against letting campaign paraphernalia distract them from engaging with delegates. “Don’t let T-shirts come between you and them. Don’t let them focus on caps and T-shirts and paraphernalia.” He said direct interaction also allowed candidates to determine whether their messages were resonating. “You don’t need the polls because you are meeting the people directly, and you can know from their reaction if your message resonates with them.” Despite his confidence, Akomea finished third in the election. He admitted the result was not what he expected. “I was expected to be first or second, not third.” He said the outcome disappointed him, although he had anticipated a difficult contest. “Yes, it disappointed me a little, but I knew it was going to be tough.” Akomea said the race was extremely close among the leading candidates. “It’s very close. The top four: 2900-something, 2900-something, 2900-something, 3000-something. It’s very close, very tight.” He also pointed to Kojo Bamba’s campaign message as a key factor in the result. “Bamba’s message was clever, very clever. His message was different.” According to Akomea, several leading candidates had largely similar campaign messages centred on experience and years of service to the party. “Basically, that was our message.” He said Bamba instead presented himself as someone who would focus on protecting delegates and the electoral process. “Bamba’s message was that these people—they’ve served the party for a long time. I don’t intend to compete with them; what I want to give you is your security. security.” He said Bamba urged delegates to support experienced candidates while giving him the role of protecting the ballot and the delegates. “So they will do the work, and I’ll just protect the ballot and protect you.”
