items.title: UN chief calls for permanent Gaza ceasefire
items.description: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday called for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks. The horrors of those attacks must never be repeated, and the ensuing hostilities in Gaza must end, Guterres said in a message marking the third anniversary. On October 7, 2023, Palestinian militant group Hamas attacked Israel from Gaza, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage. Israel responded with a war on Hamas in Gaza that killed at least 74,000 Palestinians. "The devastating hostilities that followed (the attacks) have inflicted untold suffering on Palestinians in Gaza, including massive loss of life, displacement, and destruction. Civilians continue to endure intolerable conditions. Their suffering, too, demands an end, now," said the UN chief. The ceasefire reached last year has brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace, he noted. "I urge all parties to implement their commitments in full and advance to the next phase of the ceasefire," said Guterres. "It is time for the ceasefire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law." He said that there is a need to build the political path to lasting peace across the whole region, adding that the United Nations remains unwavering in its commitment to these imperatives. "Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity, and aspirations fulfilled," said Guterres.

items.title: Nigeria since 1999: When will the years begin to count? By Dakuku Peterside
items.description: Think of a Nigerian born in 1999, the year civilian rule came back. That person is twenty-seven now. They have never lived under a military government. But they may have finished school and not found a job. They have probably learned to plan trips around insecurity, and they almost certainly run a generator at home. Democracy has been part of their whole lives. Whether it has given them any real say over that life is another matter. That is Nigeria’s Fourth Republic: civilian government has lasted, but citizens’ power over it remains uncertain. We count elections and anniversaries. We should count how often institutions protect people, public money becomes public benefit, and abuses of power carry consequences. Continuity matters. Soldiers cut short earlier republics. Since 1999, civilian rule has survived successive handovers, including 2015, when President Goodluck Jonathan lost and conceded. But survival is the beginning of democratic development, not proof of its completion. Continuity means civilian rule keeps going. Consolidation means its limits hold. Presidents accept restraint. Opposition parties compete. Judges rule without intimidation. Citizens obtain justice without a godfather. Democracy matures when these protections survive powerful people’s attempts to override them. Time alone cannot achieve that. Institutions can grow older without growing stronger. Elections may teach politicians to respect competition, or to manipulate it better. That is the continuity trap. A system that rewards insiders gives them little reason to change it. Politicians who benefit from expensive nomination forms, opaque campaign funding, and weak oversight have scant incentive to widen access. Each election that renews their influence confirms the arrangement works. What citizens experience as dysfunction, insiders regard as a successful bargain. That explains our abundant politics and shortage of service. Parties organise lavish conventions while hospitals lack medicines. Legislatures approve budgets while communities cannot identify contractors behind abandoned projects. Renewing power receives more attention than making it answerable. Institutions should correct this imbalance. Their independence has a practical test: can they act when doing so inconveniences those who appoint or fund them? The 2023 presidential election exposed the stakes. Results appeared on INEC’s Results Viewing Portal later than expected. European Union observers reported that upload failures and poor communication weakened trust. This did not itself establish fraud. It made verification harder. Courts legitimately resolve disputes, but litigation cannot replace an electoral process voters can check. Distrust discourages participation. Yet organised political machines do not withdraw alongside disappointed citizens. Staying home can strengthen the networks people distrust. Rebuilding confidence and sustaining participation go hand in hand. Democracy must also mean something in daily life. For parents choosing between food and school fees, or farmers afraid to reach their land, security and functioning services give citizenship substance. Hardship does not invalidate elected government. Difficult reforms, however, require honest explanation, fair burdens and protection for vulnerable households. The 2023 Naira redesign illustrates this. President Muhammadu Buhari acknowledged implementation difficulties in his February broadcast. The shortage of usable cash exposed the distance between official timetables and people’s capacity to cope. Reform must work for someone buying food or keeping a small business open. Leaders asking citizens to sacrifice should curb their own excesses and correct policies that fail. The “japa” debate reflects this crisis of confidence. Patriotic appeals cannot make staying worthwhile. Safety, opportunity and institutions that reward effort fairly can. Parties need open finances, credible internal contests and clear programmes. Women, young people and candidates without wealthy sponsors need realistic routes into office. Ethnic loyalty must not shield poor performance. Bringing power closer to citizens also requires safeguards: governors can abuse authority too. The Second Niger Bridge, commissioned in May 2023, shows that civilian government can deliver substantial infrastructure. The lesson is to make completion routine and maintenance dependable. Two reform demands follow. First, require publication of polling-unit result images and collation records within statutory deadlines, with documented procedures for technical failures. INEC should publish independent technical audits after elections. Breaches should attract enforceable sanctions, subject to due process. Second, give every federally funded capital project a public identifier linking its appropriation, contractor, value, payments and independently verified completion status. Publish these records quarterly on a searchable portal, with penalties for withholding or falsifying information. These measures give citizens evidence to challenge official claims between elections. Authoritarian rule offers no dependable shortcut: removing scrutiny removes tools for correcting failure. Leaders must accept safeguards that constrain them, and citizens must defend those safeguards when their preferred party governs. The generation born in 1999 deserves more than a life without soldiers in power. It deserves a government it can influence, institutions it can trust, and a country where hard work leads to a real future. We should judge the next Democracy Day by how far we have moved towards that. Nigeria has kept the clock running. Now it must make the years count. •Dr Peterside, a leadership and management expert, wrote Leading in a Storm. The post Nigeria since 1999: When will the years begin to count? By Dakuku Peterside appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: IMF talks likely to clear way for $1.2bn disbursement
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakis­tan’s ongoing talks with a visiting staff mission of the International Monet­ary Fund (IMF) are set to conclude on a positive note later this week, paving the way for the disbursement of about $1.2 billion under two concurrent progra­mmes — the $7bn Exten­ded Fund Facility (EFF) and the $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). Informed sources said the two sides were now finalising the Memor­andum of Econ­omic and Fiscal Policies (MEFP) after covering the substantive parameters of the biannual review. Following the completion of the draft exchanges, the staff mission, led by Ms Iva Petrova, is expected to conclude its visit in the next couple of days, official sources said. There were no new demands from the Fund, except for makeup adjustments to bridge past slippages. The revenue target remains unchanged, with a greater focus on achieving the half-yearly target following robust collection in the first quarter, which exceeded the target. The development comes as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict. The gas companies and the petroleum division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels. The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan. The matter has assumed greater importance because the LNG import plan will affect the current account targets agreed upon by the Ministry of Finance and the IMF. Sources, however, indicated that actual LNG imports may not exceed seven to eight cargoes over the three winter months, given prevailing market conditions, which would bring the outcome closer to the Ministry of Finance’s desired level. The two sides have agreed to expedite groundwork for targeted subsidies in the gas sector through the social protection programme to contain gas-sector circular debt and move BISP-based subsidies for the poorest consumers in the power sector into the implementation phase, starting January next year following the introduction of the revised base tariff. The distribution companies have already filed tariff petitions during the course of the talks to demonstrate their preparedness to the IMF team, the sources said. The government has assured the Fund of plans to reduce cross-subsidies from the industrial sector and contain gas-sector debt, which has now reached Rs3.6 trillion and continues to rise. This includes principal payables of around Rs1.8 trillion and almost an equivalent amount in accrued interest and late-payment surcharges. The gas companies have reported that the introduction of a protected category for domestic consumers, involving gas prices of Rs200-350 per mmBtu, has aggravated the pricing gap and, consequently, increased circular debt. Only four of the 12 consumer slabs covered the cost of gas supply during the winter months, while the remaining eight remained below breakeven rates for around eight months despite the imposition of substantial fixed charges. Although these measures are not being defined as prior actions, the authorities may have to take a few steps between the conclusion of the ongoing IMF talks and the scheduling of the Fund’s Executive Board meeting to ensure smooth processing of Pakistan’s case for the disbursement of $1.2bn and seek waivers for a couple of unavoidable slippages that had already occurred against the end-June 2026 targets. An IMF structural benchmark committed by the government requires a major policy reform by end-January 2027 to replace the budgeted tariff-differential subsidy and cross-subsidy system with a targeted, budgeted subsidy framework for low-income consumers through BISP. The World Bank is assisting the government in linking power consumers to the National Socio-Economic Registry. The government has undertaken to complete the technical linkage, along with validity checks, by end-November to determine eligibility criteria. The IMF is now also pushing for greater transparency in the Inland Freight Equalisation Margin (IFEM), which facilitates uniform petroleum pricing across the country. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

NPP wants early profiling of parliamentary candidates to avoid costly campaigns – Nana Akomea
items.description: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) plans to profile potential parliamentary candidates early in constituencies without sitting MPs to prevent aspirants from spending heavily on campaigns that may ultimately fail. Newly elected Third Vice Chairperson of the NPP, Nana Akomea, says the party now has enough time to deliberately assess the demographics of these constituencies before settling on suitable candidates. He said the approach would be particularly important because the NPP now has more constituencies without sitting MPs. “But what is essential is the demography. We have a bit of time now to look at the demography of each of the orphan constituencies.” Nana Akomea said constituency-level demographic reports would help the party determine which type of candidate would have the best chance of winning. “The constituency party will bring us reports about the demography, and they would suggest that for this constituency, if we get a candidate from this demography, it will help us.” He said making that assessment early would prevent potential aspirants from investing heavily in campaigns before the party determines who is best positioned to win. “So when that determination is done early, then somebody who is not from that demography will not go and waste time to go and campaign, spend money, and then later on you decide that oh, he may not win.” Nana Akomea said such a situation could become more complicated because aspirants would already have built support networks and developed emotional ties to their campaigns. “But then he’s already invested money. He’s already got followers. His emotions involved.” He argued that the strategy is not entirely new to the NPP. “In the NPP going to the 2000 elections, we did the same exercise. We had a lot of constituencies with no sitting MPs, and we decided that the coastal area of Accra, for example, should be reserved for Gas.” “That is profiling, and so on. So it is not new.” The difference, he said, is the scale and the deliberate nature of the current exercise. “It’s that we’re going to do it on a scale that is more deliberate and that is more fulfilling.” Nana Akomea also linked the strategy to the NPP’s decision to complete its internal reorganisation early. He said the party had “secured for ourselves the blessing of time” by selecting its flagbearer well ahead of the 2028 elections. According to him, that early decision has helped reduce internal tensions and created room for the party to focus on parliamentary preparations. “Now there isn’t any emotion because we’ve already settled that high price. So we’ve composed ourselves.” He said the party’s next major task is to get its parliamentary strategy right, particularly in constituencies without sitting MPs. “What we need to do now is to get the parliamentary thing right. There are a lot more orphan constituencies. You don’t want to leave it free for all.” He said the available time should allow the NPP to be more deliberate about who represents the party in those constituencies. “Now that we have a bit of time, you can be more deliberate about the people to represent the party in the constituencies.”

items.title: Edo’s special court sends clear message: Justice must catch up with kidnappers, by Ejiro Ofoye
items.description: The fight against kidnapping and violent crime in Nigeria has often suffered from one debilitating weakness: the distance between arrest and justice. Suspects are arrested, paraded before television cameras, arraigned in court and then, in too many cases, disappear into years of adjournments and procedural delays. For victims and their families, justice becomes an uncertain promise. That is why the judgment delivered on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, by the Edo State Special Criminal Court in Benin City deserves serious national attention. Justice Aigbona Momodu sentenced four defendants — Marvellous Isaac, Wisdom Michael, Rufus Emete Michael and Gift Raphael — to death on several counts arising from a broad-daylight kidnapping at the Vegetable Market along Airport Road, Benin City. The 11-count case included kidnapping, conspiracy, armed robbery, cultism and unlawful possession of firearms. The case is particularly significant because it represents the maiden kidnapping judgment of Edo State’s Special Criminal Court, established to deal specifically with kidnapping, cultism and related violent offences. The court commenced operations in July 2026 following a request from Governor Monday Okpebholo to the Chief Judge of Edo State for a special court to accelerate the determination of such cases. This is where Justice Momodu deserves recognition — not because he imposed the death penalty as a matter of personal preference, but because his judgment demonstrated an important principle of constitutional democracy: a judge must apply the law, even when the consequences are severe. Indeed, the judge made it clear that the sentence was dictated by the applicable law. “My hands are tied under the law,” he said, explaining that he would have exercised discretion if the law permitted him to do so. That statement is perhaps one of the most important aspects of the judgment. A judge is not a political actor. A judge does not determine punishment according to public anger, political pressure or personal sentiment. Where legislation prescribes a particular punishment for an offence and the prosecution has established the case beyond reasonable doubt, the court’s responsibility is to apply the law. In this case, Isaac received seven years’ imprisonment on one count, death sentences on counts two to nine, 10 years on another count and life imprisonment on the final count. The other three defendants also received death sentences on the counts for which they were convicted, alongside additional terms of imprisonment. Interestingly, the formal wording of the judgment referred to death “by hanging or through the administration of a lethal injection.” The court nevertheless went on to pronounce the traditional formula that the convicts should be hanged by the neck until dead. The significance of the wording should not be lost. Under Nigeria’s criminal law, the traditional statutory formulation provides for death by hanging, while the law also sets out procedures following a death sentence, including transmission of the judgment to the appropriate executive authority. A death sentence, therefore, should not be confused with an immediate execution. The Nigerian legal system provides procedures following the imposition of capital punishment, and condemned persons retain whatever appellate and constitutional remedies are available to them under the law. But beyond the punishment itself, there is another issue Nigerians should examine: the speed with which the Edo justice system has moved this particular case. The alleged kidnapping occurred on June 14, 2026. By September 29, the special court had delivered its judgment. That does not mean every kidnapping case can or should be concluded within the same period. Each case has its own facts, evidence and procedural requirements. But it demonstrates what can happen when specialised judicial attention is combined with focused prosecution and investigative work. The Edo State Government also deserves recognition for placing the issue of kidnapping and violent crime prominently within its security agenda. In June, following the Airport Road kidnapping, Governor Okpebholo requested the creation of a special court for kidnapping and cultism cases. The Chief Judge subsequently constituted the Special Criminal Court. There is also an important precedent concerning armed robbery. In May 2025, the Edo State Government announced that the Supreme Court had affirmed the conviction and death sentence of Sunday Osakpolor for armed robbery. The state also reported the conviction of Taiwo Omorede and four others in another armed robbery case, with three receiving death sentences by hanging and two receiving five-year prison terms. These developments show that the present judgment did not emerge in isolation. There has been an established effort by the Edo Ministry of Justice to prosecute serious violent offences through the courts. But the real test is what happens next. Justice must not end with sentencing. The prosecution must remain diligent. Police investigations must be professional. Evidence must be properly preserved. Victims and witnesses must be protected. Appeals must be handled according to law. And the executive authorities must respect the constitutional procedures governing capital punishment. Most importantly, Edo must ensure that the special court does not become merely a symbol. Its success should ultimately be measured by whether it consistently delivers speedy, fair and lawful justice across kidnapping and cultism cases. For the families of kidnapping victims, the message from the Benin courtroom is simple: the law can still catch up with those who use violence to terrorise citizens. Justice Momodu’s judgment has shown the importance of a judiciary that applies the law without fear or favour. The Edo Government’s creation of a specialised judicial mechanism has also demonstrated the potential value of giving serious criminal cases dedicated judicial attention. The larger lesson for Nigeria is even clearer: the fight against kidnapping cannot be won by rhetoric alone. Arrests must lead to credible investigations, investigations must lead to prosecution, prosecution must lead to fair trials, and where guilt is established, punishment must follow the law. That is how the criminal justice chain is supposed to work. And that is how public confidence in the rule of law is rebuilt. The post Edo’s special court sends clear message: Justice must catch up with kidnappers, by Ejiro Ofoye appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: At least 22 dead after two boats collide on Congo river, official says
items.description: At least 22 people have died after two boats collided on the Congo River ​in the Democratic Republic of Congo, an ‌official said. The incident occurred near the town of Ngombe in Lukolela territory in western Equateur province at around 2 ​a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on Saturday, Crispin ​Mputu, the provincial interior minister, told Reuters. The Reuters Daily Briefing newsletter provides all the news you need to start your day. Sign up here. The ⁠collision involved two vessels travelling on the river. ​One was a commercial boat operating between Kinshasa ​and Mbandaka, while the other was a passenger riverboat travelling from Mongala province to Kinshasa, Mputu said. The impact ​caused the passenger boat to sink. A security ​source told Reuters it had 163 passengers on board. Twenty-two bodies ‌have ⁠been recovered and buried, while 59 people were rescued, Mputu said. He added that other victims might have been buried elsewhere. The sunken vessel ​remains submerged at ​a depth ⁠of 12 meters and recovery efforts were continuing on Monday evening, ​Mputu said. River transport is the main form ​of ⁠travel and trade in much of western Congo, where towns and cities are located along the ⁠Congo River, ​but accidents are common because ​vessels are often overcrowded and poorly maintained.

The Interior Ministry reported deaths and injuries ​in Dakar and the northeastern town of ​Matam. It said a building had collapsed in the ‌southern ⁠town of Kaolack. Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo said there was a high probability of more rain on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday He also said ​this week’s ​start of ⁠the school year could be postponed if floodwaters did not recede. items.title: Why Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway (3), by Eric Teniola
items.description: This week continues the narrative on Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway. No doubt that region has contributed a lot to modern-day Nigeria. Their leaders too, some of whom are alive while some are deceased, have served to make this country a great one. I think we owe them a debt of gratitude. I don’t think we can compensate them enough for their services. I will name a few at the risk of offending many. We have Professor Eyo Ita (1903–1972), Ernest Sesei Ikoli (1893–1960), Dr. Kenule Beeson Saro-Wiwa (10 October 1941 – 10 November 1995), Major Isaac Jasper Adaka Boro (September 10, 1938 – 9 May 1968), Chief Edwin Clarke (May 25, 1927 – February 17, 2025), Chief Eyo Ita Esua (1901–1973), Dr. Clement Isong (April 20, 1920 – 29 May 2000), Dr. Joseph Wayas, GCON (21 May 1941 – 30 November 2021), Chief Anthony Eromosele Enahoro (22 July 1923 – 15 December 2010), Chief Godswill Akpabio (63), GCON, Chief Arthur Edwin Prest (1906–1976) and Sir Festus Okotie-Eboh (18 July 1912 – 15 January 1966). Others are Former President Goodluck Jonathan (68), GCFR, Chief Ufot Ekaette (17 April 1939 – 25 September 2019), Chief Allison Akene Ayida (June 16, 1930 – October 12, 2018), King Jaja of Opobo (1821–1891), Chief Douglas, Amanyanabo of Opobo (1915–1980), Professor Horatio Oritsejolomi Thomas (1917–1979), Dr. Udo Udoma (21 June 1917 – 2 February 1998), Chief Humphrey Omo-Osagie (1896–1977), Chief Michael Ani (30 November 1917 – 18 December 1985), Sir Dennis Osadebay (29 June 1911 — 26 December 1994), Dr. Okoi Arikpo (20 September 1916 – 26 October 1995), Chief Wenike Opurum Briggs (10 March 1918 – 21 April 1987), Chief Harold Dappa-Biriye (26 September 1920 – 2005), Chief Louis Orok Edet (1914–1979), Chief Margaret Ekpo and many others. Let us take a look at some of them. Professor Eyo Ita (1903–1972) was the founder of the Nigeria Youth League Movement. He was born in Calabar. He had his education at Duke Town School and then went to Calabar’s famous Hope Waddell Training Institute. After teaching at the Baptist Academy, Obanikoro, Lagos (1926–1928), he went to the USA where he studied at the Teacher’s College of Columbia University, majoring in religion and education. He later read for a BA in Canada. On his return in 1933, he became active as an educationist, a pamphleteer, and a nationalist who believed strongly in a role for Nigeria’s youth. He formed the Nigeria Youth League Movement, which had little effective existence at first. After spending some time at Ogbomoso, where he taught but also wrote pamphlets and press articles, he returned in 1938 to Calabar, where a National Institute had been founded by local educated people, and he became its head. Then he started his own West African People’s Institute, an educational institution for which he became famous. It had a press which published his works: The Assurance of Freedom (1949), Crusade for Freedom (1949), The Revolt of the Liberal Spirit in Nigeria (1949), Sterile Truths and Fertile Lies (1949), Two Vital Fronts in Nigeria’s Advancement (1949), National Youth Renaissance (undated), Theory of Social Symbiosis (1951), etc. Chief Eyo Ita was a leading member of the National Council for Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) after its foundation in 1944, and was elected to the Eastern Nigeria House of Assembly in 1951 on the party’s ticket. In 1948 he became the first National Vice-President of the NCNC. After elections in 1951, which the NCNC won in the Eastern Region, he became Minister for Natural Resources and Leader of Government Business for the Region. A year later there was a crisis within the NCNC; in January 1953, the nine NCNC ministers in the East resigned, but Chief Ita and five others withdrew their resignations and stayed as ministers despite a hostile House of Assembly, until new elections in the same year installed a government under the NCNC leader, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe. Before that, Chief Eyo Ita had formed a National Independence Party (NIP) with Dr. E.U. Udoma and Jaja Wachukwu. Later in 1953 the Calabar-Ogoja-Rivers (COR) movement was founded to call for separation of the non-Ibo minorities from the Eastern Region, and Chief Ita was one of the leading figures for some years. Later his NIP joined the United National Party (UNP) of Alvan Ikoku to form the National Independence Party. In 1959 he announced he was leaving the COR movement and returned to the NCNC. The “Professor”, as he was called, was not prominent in politics thereafter. After independence he devoted his time to developing and improving his school. Chief Ernest Sesei Ikoli (1893–1960) was born on 25 March 1893 in Rivers State. He was the son of an illustrious merchant who traded on the coast of south-east Nigeria. His mother was among the first women from the Niger Delta to receive Western education. He had his education at the Bonny Primary School and then King’s College in Lagos, where he was one of the foundation students on its opening in 1909; later he taught there, becoming assistant Mathematics master in 1913. After resigning from King’s College in 1919, he went into journalism as editorial assistant at the Lagos Weekly Record under the editorship of Thomas Horatio Jackson, who had taken over from his father, John Payne Jackson, who founded the paper in 1889. After two years with the Record, Ikoli founded his own newspaper, the African Messenger, in 1921. He remained its editor and proprietor until 1926 when he was appointed the first editor of the newly founded DAILY TIMES, whose first editorial he wrote on 1 June 1926. The previous year the Daily Times had taken over Ikoli’s African Messenger. In 1928 he left the Daily Times to found THE NIGERIAN DAILY until 1931 when it ceased publication. Chief Ernest Ikoli also took part in politics in Lagos, starting as secretary of the local branch of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) of Marcus Garvey. items.title: Phishing domains impersonate govt agencies
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The National Cyber Security Emergency Response Team (NCERT) has detected a number of suspected phishing domains created in the name of key national institutions, apparently aimed at stealing sensitive information from citizens. According to the NCERT’s Threat Intelligence Centre, suspicious domains impersonating several government and public sector organisations were found active on Sunday (Oct 4). The identified domains include a suspected “secure login” domain impersonating the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra), while phishing domains using names like the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), the Higher Education Commission (HEC), the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) were also detected. Likewise, suspicious domains impersonating the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP), the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) and the Prime Minister’s Youth Programme were identified. NCERT advises public not to share personal information on unauthorised websites The Threat Intelligence Centre also spotted a suspicious login domain using the name of Punjab Safe Cities. The NCERT said the suspected phishing domains were still active and their activities were being monitored. It warned that phishing websites and impersonation-based attacks could be used to deceive users into entering sensitive information, including login credentials and other personal data. The NCERT advised citizens and government organisations to exercise caution while accessing links, websites and login pages received through unverified sources. It urged users to verify the authenticity of websites before entering personal information and said monitoring of phishing activities and impersonation of national institutions was in progress. Safe use of GenAI At the same time, National Cert has issued an advisory for “safe and secure use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools and platforms”. The rapid adoption of public AI chatbots, coding assistants, browser extensions, AI-enabled applications, and third-party AI services is creating new cybersecurity and data governance risks across organisations, the agency observed. It added that uncontrolled or unauthorised use of Generative AI, commonly referred to as Shadow AI, may expose sensitive information, intellectual property, credentials, source code, and organisational data while introducing risks from prompt injection, insecure AI-generated code, malicious integrations, inaccurate outputs, and compromised third-party models. The NCERT has advised organisations to protect “sensitive and classified information, strictly prohibit the submission of classified, confidential, sensitive, personal, proprietary, credential-related, or otherwise restricted organisational information to public or unapproved AI platforms. Organisations have been directed to establish an approved AI tool registry, while maintaining a centrally vetted and regularly reviewed inventory of authorised AI tools, models, browser extensions, plug-ins, APIs, and platforms. The advice added that organisations should remain on the vigil for sensitive data exposure, Shadow AI, unauthorised AI plug-ins, suspicious AI access and policy violations. The cybersecurity agency added that wherever an AI-related incident occurs, organisations should immediately contain unauthorised access. Organisations were also advised to preserve evidence and logs, revoke compromised credentials or API keys, investigate exposure, implement corrective measures and report the incident to the NCERT. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

items.title: Eku festival: When cutlasses dance, families mourn,
items.description: •Some renamed it ‘Feast of blood’ •20 killed in 2 decades — Oniovosa By Jimitota Onoyume, Assistant News Editor For generations, the Urhobo community of Eku in Ethiope East Local Government Area of Delta State counted down the days to their annual festival like Christians awaiting Christmas. Families of the predominantly Baptist community scattered across the country would return home. Music would spill from every corner. The various quarters would gather in colourful displays of cultural heritage and pride. It was a time to celebrate, to reunite, to remember who they were. But something has changed. The drums still beat, the cutlasses still flash, but now they carry a darker meaning. Some natives no longer call it a festival. They nicknamed it the “Eku Feast of Blood.” Andrew, a sexagenarian and son of the soil, speaks with the weariness of a man who has seen too many young bodies carried away. He says at least 15 people have been killed during the festival in the past two decades.”We used to look forward to the festival,” he says quietly, his voice barely above a whisper. “Now, parents worry about whether their children will return home alive.” He stressed this with the gravity of a man who has seen too many funerals of youths. Another resident, Oniovosa, puts the figure higher, saying more than 20 had died in the last 20 years. This year, that fear came true again. Last Monday, while the town was still swaying to the rhythm of celebration, word spread like wildfire: three youths had been killed in the community. They had been part of the festivities. Within minutes, graphic photographs and videos flooded social media, turning a day of joy into one of grief, panic and disbelief. For a member of Isaac’s family, one of the deceased who rode Okada to help himself, the tragedy cut deepest. In a video that has since broken hearts across the state, she wailed uncontrollably, recalling how she had warned him before he left home. He had told her he was going to Osuere, the geographical centre of the community before its expansion, with a friend to have fun. “He is gone, he is gone,” she cried. “Isaac, mevuewo o memera. Isaac, I told you to be careful as you were going.” What felt like an ordinary warning became a final goodbye. The words echo now in the empty home. The circumstances of the killings remain unclear, with conflicting accounts emerging. Some claimed it was a supremacy battle between rival groups. Others insisted it had nothing to do with cultism. “ This thing is spiritual, whether you blame it on cultism or not, for me it is spiritually manipulated,” one youth said, his voice trembling with frustration. “People should stop giving every killing in our community the same explanation without investigating what truly happened,” he stressed. According to some accounts, a man received a phone call that a member of his group had been shot elsewhere. And he allegedly grabbed a pump-action rifle and later opened fire on three youths. How true the foregoing is, the Police will tell at the end of its investigation. The Police are still investigating, but for the families of the dead, no investigation can bring back their sons. The violence did not end with gunshots. About five others were rushed to different hospitals in the local government area with deep cutlass wounds. Kenneth, a resident, explained that cutlasses are part of the traditional festival; youths dance with them to display strength and bravery. “But if you cut someone , the person may retaliate,” he says, his eyes reflecting a mixture of tradition and tragedy. “A small disagreement can quickly become a serious fight.” One of the deceased killed that black Monday was found with a cutlass injury around the neck, a grim testament to how a symbol of heritage has become an instrument of death. For years, deaths at the festival have been dismissed as cult clashes. But residents say no one has allegedly been convicted over the killing. Some tried to link this latest tragedy to politics, but that was quickly rejected. The post Eku festival: When cutlasses dance, families mourn, appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Sri Lanka: Counterterrorism Bill Retains Abusive Powers
items.description: Click to expand Image A police officer holds handcuffs as he walks inside a court premises in Colombo, Sri Lanka, August 6, 2026. © 2026 Thilina Kaluthotage/Reuters (Brussels) – The Sri Lankan government’s latest attempt to replace its abusive Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) retains numerous provisions that have enabled serious human rights violations, Human Rights Watch said today. The proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTB), which will be sent to Parliament on October 6, 2026, includes an overbroad definition of terrorism, inadequate judicial oversight, sweeping powers of search and arrest for the armed forces, and executive authority to curtail freedom of speech, assembly, association, and movement. These provisions neither meet the benchmarks set out by United Nations human rights experts, nor comply with human rights obligations and commitments that Sri Lanka made to the European Union under the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP+), which links trade benefits to human rights conditions. “Sri Lankan authorities have long used draconian counterterrorism legislation to persecute minorities and target the victims of rights abuses and activists seeking justice and accountability,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The proposed law will allow similar abuses, breaching Sri Lanka’s obligations under international law and jeopardizing its EU trade benefits.” President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s National People’s Power alliance pledged in its 2024 election manifesto to campaign for the abolition “of all oppressive acts including the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) and ensuring civil rights of people in all parts of the country.” The bill is the proposed replacement for the PTA, which has enabled arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, and torture. That law—first enacted in 1979 as a “temporary” measure—has been used to target Tamil and Muslim communities, the media, human rights defenders, and others critical of successive governments, entrenching impunity in Sri Lanka for 46 years. In 2017, Sri Lanka committed to repealing the PTA as a condition for the EU to reinstate its GSP+ status. Since 2018, several attempts to repeal and replace the PTA have failed. The government introduced an earlier version of the bill in late 2025, but it was withdrawn and has been reintroduced with some changes following criticism by human rights groups, media, and others. Meanwhile, despite the government’s pledge to abolish the PTA, the Dissanayake government continued to use the law. In June 2026 it was used to arrest and detain Sangeethan Ganeshkumar, a 24-year-old Tamil hip-hop artist, in connection with a music video. According to information provided to the UN by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, there were 46 PTA-related detention cases in 2025 and 12 in the first 3 months of 2026. It has at times been used in cases—such as alleged organized crime—that should be addressed using ordinary criminal laws, not counterterrorism authority. In 2021, UN human rights experts set out five prerequisites to ensure that any proposed counterterrorism law complies with international human rights standards. They include providing a definition of terrorism that complies with international norms to ensure precision and legal certainty, especially when the legislation may affect the rights of freedom of expression, opinion, peaceful assembly, association, and religion or belief; instituting robust measures to prevent and halt arbitrary deprivation of liberty; ensuring measures to prevent torture and enforced disappearance; and enabling overarching due process and fair trial guarantees, including judicial oversight and access to legal counsel. The bill does not meet these standards, Human Rights Watch said. The draft law includes broad and vague definitions of terrorism and could undermine the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The definition of terrorism problematically includes “unduly compelling a government or an international organization, to do or to abstain from doing any act.” The bill also includes a sweeping provision that anyone who, with “intention or knowledge…directly or indirectly,” induces any person to commit, attempt, abet, conspire to commit, or prepare to commit, the offense of “terrorism” by “distributing, circulating,” or providing “a service to others that enables them to obtain, read, listen to or look at a terrorist publication” commits an offense. The risk that this authority could be used to curtail free speech is shown by the repeated use of the PTA to interrogate, arrest, and detain journalists and social media users. While the definitions of offenses under the bill are overbroad, the bill includes some improvements. It provides that those who engage in protest, advocacy or dissent; industrial or labor action; or humanitarian and medical assistance will not be considered to commit an offense. However, this does not adequately address the dangers contained in other clauses that could result in abuse. A further serious concern, as with the previous counterterrorism drafts, is that the latest bill provides broad authority to Sri Lanka’s police, armed forces, and coast guard with “reasonable suspicion” to stop, search, question, enter premises, and take suspects into custody without a warrant. The proposed law enables the inspector general of police or a deputy inspector general of police to obtain an order from the defense secretary to detain a suspect for two months, which can be extended up to a year. A magistrate cannot overturn a detention order, removing effective judicial oversight. Using different provisions under the bill, a person could be held without charge for up to a total of two years. The bill provides some safeguards, such as allowing a magistrate to visit approved detention sites without notice, interview detainees, and direct officials to bring detainees before a Judicial Medical Officer if there is suspicion of torture or ill-treatment. The magistrate can also order a change of detention site. The bill provides for an Independent Review Committee appointed by the defense minister to review the “necessity, legality and proportionality” of a detention order within 30 days and recommend to the minister whether it should be confirmed, varied, or revoked. While independent reviews of detention orders could reduce abuses, the committee’s appointment by the minister would place the independence of such scrutiny in doubt. Finally, the proposed law grants sweeping government authority to curtail freedom of movement and association, including for the president to proscribe organizations without judicial oversight. The defense secretary is empowered to designate anywhere a “prohibited place,” while a deputy inspector general of police can obtain a court order to restrict an individual’s movement and communications for up to three months. Such broad powers with limited or no judicial oversight would have a chilling effect on free speech, association, assembly, and movement. The Sri Lankan government should impose an immediate moratorium on the use of the PTA while it comprehensively amends the PTSB or prepares a new bill that meets international standards, Human Rights Watch said. “Sri Lanka has a grim history of misusing bad counterterrorism laws to commit serious human rights violations, and this bill would do little to stop that from happening again,” Pearson said. “The Sri Lankan government should fulfill its international legal obligations and commitments to the EU and other international partners by legislating to end these abuses instead of simply repackaging the same abusive powers in new legislation.”

items.title: Vieillissement : l’OCDE appelle les pays en développement à renforcer leurs systèmes de retraite
items.description: Le vieillissement devient un défi de plus en plus urgent dans les pays en développement, dans un contexte où « le niveau d’informalité reste élevé », a relevé l'Organisation de coopération et de développement économiques (OCDE) dans son dernier rapport sur l'économie informelle publié lundi. Dans ce rapport intitulé « Assurer les moyens de subsistance des travailleurs de l'économie informelle à l'heure des changements mondiaux », l'OCDE note que les pays en développement connaissent « des transitions démographiques beaucoup plus rapides que celles qu'ont connues historiquement les pays développés », mettant en garde que leurs systèmes de retraite « ne couvrent souvent pas de manière adéquate les travailleurs du secteur informel ». En moyenne, parmi les pays couverts par le rapport, seuls 51 % des personnes ayant dépassé l'âge légal de la retraite perçoivent une pension, tandis que seulement 40 % des travailleurs cotisent à un régime de retraite. En conséquence, de nombreuses personnes âgées continuent de travailler dans le secteur informel au-delà de l'âge de la retraite ou dépendent du soutien familial, détaille le document. Le rapport constate, néanmoins, qu'il est possible d'étendre la couverture des retraites dans les économies à forte composante informelle, même pour les pays qui sont sur le point de devenir des sociétés « vieillissantes », notamment l'Indonésie, le Mexique, le Pérou, la Thaïlande ou le Vietnam. Pour ce qui est des pays africains, il relève qu'ils disposent de plus de temps pour se préparer, bien que certains d'entre eux sont bien placés pour mettre en place des systèmes solides, suggérant que des retraites sociales universelles pourraient, par exemple, être financées par des réformes fiscales à un coût budgétaire relativement faible. Le rapport examine l'impact de l’emploi informel non seulement sur les travailleurs eux-mêmes, mais aussi dans les ménages et sur les personnes à leur charge, dans les économies en développement et émergentes, alors que 55 % de la population des 58 pays étudiés – en Afrique, en Amérique, en Asie et en Europe – vit dans des ménages entièrement informels. Dans ce document, l'OCDE s'intéresse de plus près aux personnes derrière les statistiques — notamment les femmes, les travailleurs peu qualifiés et les personnes âgées — et explore la manière dont l'économie informelle interagit avec trois tendances mondiales susceptibles d’aggraver les vulnérabilités existantes : le vieillissement de la population, l'automatisation et la dégradation de l'environnement, telle que les sécheresses, les inondations ou les vagues de chaleur. The post Vieillissement : l’OCDE appelle les pays en développement à renforcer leurs systèmes de retraite appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Thèse amphigourique
items.description: Dans un « papier » dont il a le secret, le directeur de la rédaction de Jeune Afrique, François Soudan, véritable mercenaire de la plume (les témoignages émanant des palais présidentiels africains l’atteste) tente de rapprocher le nationalisme libérateur du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, à celui expansionniste et chauviniste des extrêmes droites occidentales principalement celles américaine et française dont les porte-voix sont actuellement Donald Trump et Marine le Pen. Une thèse amphigourique et auto-suggérée si tant est qu’il y a loin de la coupe aux lèvres s’agissant de ces deux modèles de gouvernement. Faut-il le rappeler, la doctrine politique du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré est basée sur la libération d’un peuple, celui burkinabè, soumis jusque-là à une domination étrangère sans pour autant faire preuve d’ostracisme à l’endroit des autres peuples épris de cet idéal noble. A contrario, le nationalisme expansionniste de Trump et le Pen vise à affirmer le primat de leurs peuples sur les autres ce qui en fait un « avatar » de l’impérialisme avec de forts relents racistes. Dans sa volonté de pervertir le discours du président du Faso, qui irradie de plus en plus l’ensemble de la planète, Jeune Afrique n’hésite pas à s’accrocher à cette branche pourrie des sciences politiques, persuadée que le niveau de conscience politique des masses africaines n’est pas assez élevé pour percevoir ce lavage de cerveau. Un exercice futile d’une vacuité sans pareille dans un continent qui se réveille et qui accorde peu d’intérêt aux sirènes d’outre-mer. Un exercice de style qui finit par révéler son vrai objectif quand ce plumitif stipendié par ses maîtres de l’ombre, pousse l’outrecuidance jusqu’à affirmer que les pays de l’AES devraient se satisfaire de l’avènement au pouvoir de Marine le Pen, car cela signifierait la fin de la menace impérialiste ; Dame le Pen étant selon lui adepte de la préférence nationale. Une manière de nous endormir quand on sait que la « préférence nationale » française ne peut prospérer en dehors de l’Afrique francophone où elle puise l’essentiel des ressources nécessaires à sa survie. Quel que soit le gouvernement qui dirigera la France, il constituera toujours une menace pour nous au vu de cette relation dialectique. Le président du Faso l’a du reste indiqué, « l’hiver noir n’a pas encore commencé » et, l’alerte rouge doit être permanente. Ce nouveau narratif où se mêlent flatterie, condescendance et roublardise (de France-Afrique il est question maintenant d’Afrique France) ne saurait prospérer, car, personne ne boit l’eau par les narines désormais. Alors, allez-vous rhabiller messieurs les sophistes. Boubakar SY

items.title: journées nationales d’engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne : le message du Président du Faso
items.description: Camarades, Il y a six mois, je vous invitais à regarder au fond de votre assiette. « Mon assiette, ma fierté », tel était le mot d’ordre. Aujourd’hui, dans la continuité du thème général de la IIIe édition des Journées Nationales d’Engagement Patriotique et de Participation Citoyenne, « Produisons burkinabè, consommons burkinabè ! », je vous invite à aller plus loin. Pour cette phase 2, voici le nouveau mot d’ordre : « Tous pour le Made in Burkina : Faisons de chaque achat un acte de souveraineté ». Car c’est de nos champs, de nos ateliers, de nos boutiques et de nos tables que se construit une nation debout, fière et souveraine. Notre peuple doit produire, transformer et consommer. Ce sont les trois maillons d’une même chaîne. Qu’un seul cède, et c’est toute la chaîne qui se fragilise. Si nous ne produisons pas, si nous ne transformons pas, si nous ne consommons pas ce qui vient de chez nous, d’autres nous nourriront et nous habilleront. Or, souvenons-nous de cette vérité : celui qui vous nourrit finit par vous dicter sa volonté. Camarades, disons-nous la vérité : trois verrous maintiennent encore notre dépendance. Le premier verrou, c’est la production. Les bras valides ne manquent pas dans nos villes et nos campagnes. La terre est féconde. Mais l’eau dort encore dans nos barrages. Les tracteurs ne sillonnent pas assez nos champs. Les semences et les engrais restent insuffisants et arrivent parfois tard. L’insécurité qui nous a été imposée a éloigné des familles entières de leurs terres. Pourtant, partout où nous avons aménagé et soutenu la production, la terre a répondu : plus de sept millions de tonnes de céréales et le cap du million de tonnes de riz franchi. La preuve est là : le Burkina Faso peut se nourrir lui-même. Le deuxième verrou, c’est la transformation. C’est là que nous devons franchir un cap décisif. Nous vendons encore trop souvent brut, et nous rachetons fini. Le coton ne doit plus quitter notre pays en balles pour nous revenir en chemises. Le karité ne doit plus partir en amandes pour nous revenir, après transformation ailleurs, en pommades, en crèmes ou en chocolat vendus à prix d’or. Il en va de même du sésame, de la mangue, des cuirs et des peaux, du bétail sur pied : chaque fois que nous exportons sans transformer, nous transférons ailleurs la plus grande part de notre richesse. La valeur ajoutée n’est pas un mot d’économiste : ce sont des emplois pour nos jeunes, des revenus pour nos familles, des ressources pour nos écoles. Et pendant ce temps, ce que nous ne savons ni sécher, ni conserver, ni emballer pourrit dans nos villages. Un pays qui ne transforme pas ses richesses, en cède la plus grande valeur aux autres. Le troisième verrou, c’est la consommation. Celui-là n’est ni dans nos champs ni dans nos usines : il est dans nos têtes. Le riz importé a longtemps inondé nos marchés pendant que le riz de Bagré, du Sourou et de Samendeni cherchait preneur. Le bouillon industriel dispute sa place au soumbala dans nos sauces. Du Faso Dan Fani, on dit qu’il est « cher » ; de la chemise importée, on dit qu’elle est « normale ». Ce conditionnement doit être brisé. Servir ce que notre terre a produit n’est pas un signe de pauvreté. C’est un acte de fierté, un geste d’honneur, une affirmation de souveraineté. Chers camarades, chacun de nous doit accomplir sa part dans la bataille pour le consommer national. Camarades paysans, nous voulons faire de vous des acteurs économiques puissants : organisés, bien outillés, justement rémunérés, et pleinement conscients de votre rôle. Nous nous battons pour des prix rémunérateurs et pour que vos récoltes trouvent rapidement des débouchés. Le paysan burkinabè n’est pas un assisté : il est le premier combattant de notre souveraineté. Rien ne se transforme, rien ne se consomme, si ses mains n’ont pas d’abord produit. Camarades femmes, productrices, transformatrices, commerçantes, tisseuses, gardiennes de nos cuisines. Vous êtes au cœur des trois maillons de la chaîne : la production, la transformation et la consommation. Partout s’exprime votre génie créateur, aussi bien dans la production du soumbala que dans celle du dèguè, des farines infantiles, du beurre de karité, du Faso Dan Fani. Le camarade Thomas SANKARA l’avait dit avant nous : « Il faut donc consommer burkinabè. Et pour consommer burkinabè, la meilleure arme, ce sont les femmes. Si les femmes ne sont pas d’accord, si les femmes sont pro-impérialistes, les repas seront pro-impérialistes ! Si les femmes sont décidées à boycotter les produits importés, alors c’est la garantie ! […] En libérant le génie créateur de nos femmes, nous libérons notre économie. » Tout est dit : une partie de notre souveraineté se joue jusque dans la marmite. Camarades forestiers, rappelons-le, « la lutte contre la désertification ne peut se dissocier de la lutte anti impérialiste ». Il n’y a pas d’assiette pleine sur une terre morte. Celui qui plante un arbre, protège les sols et restaure les terres. Celui la produit autant que celui qui sème. Reboiser, camarades, c’est produire. Aujourd’hui, nous devons reverdir le Burkina Faso : nos rues, nos quartiers, nos villages, nos habitations. Voulons-nous épargner à nos enfants une part des affres du réchauffement climatique ? Alors plantons des arbres partout. Planter un arbre est un acte révolutionnaire. Camarades artisans, commerçants et industriels, le jour où le peuple a décidé de porter le Faso Dan Fani et le Kôkô Dunda, ceux-là mêmes qui importaient se sont mis à en vendre, parce que leur marchandise ne s’écoulait plus. Le commerçant a donc un choix : être le relais de la production nationale ou l’auxiliaire de la dépendance étrangère. Choisissez votre camp. Quant à nos transformateurs et transformatrices, faites grandir nos capacités de transformation, de l’atelier à la manufacture, et de la manufacture à l’usine, puis portez nos produits jusqu’au marché, sous le label « Made in Burkina ». Chers camarades, cette bataille a ses ennemis, et je les nomme sans détour. La fraude, la contrebande, et les fausses déclarations font entrer à vil prix des produits qui concurrencent déloyalement ce que nos unités produisent honnêtement. Il y a le commerçant véreux qui spécule sur la faim, cache les vivres pour faire monter les prix ou dénigre nos produits pour écouler ceux importés. Il y a le saboteur qui pratique la rétention de stocks, diffuse des rumeurs sur la qualité de nos productions ou provoque des retards volontaires de livraison. Il y a enfin ceux qui contournent la préférence nationale dans les marchés publics. Toutes ces pratiques affaiblissent notre production et doivent être combattues sans relâche. Plus insidieux encore : le boycott silencieux. Ceux qui applaudissent le consommer national en public et remplissent leur table de produits importés en privé. Ceux qui écrivent « Made in Burkina » dans leurs discours et refusent dans leurs bons de commande, d’inclure des produits burkinabè. A ceux-là, je le dis clairement : vous trahissez le combat que vous prétendez servir. Nous poursuivrons la normalisation de nos produits transformés, la protection du label national et la lutte contre les pratiques frauduleuses. Mais aucune loi, aucun contrôle ne remplacera la vigilance du peuple. Je demande donc à chacun d’être vigilant, d’être un « labaal » de cette bataille pour notre souveraineté économique. Chers camarades, chacun à son poste, chacun selon ses responsabilités, je vous appelle à faire sauter ces verrous un à un : 1) Pour produire : l’Offensive agropastorale et halieutique, la mécanisation, les aménagements hydro-agricoles, les intrants et nos coopératives villageoises sont des instruments au service du peuple. Servez-vous-en pleinement ! 2) Pour transformer : nos unités industrielles du riz, de la tomate, du karité et du coton ; la normalisation, l’emballage, la labellisation et la protection du « Made in Burkina » sont en marche, accélérons encore ces initiatives ! 3) Pour consommer : faisons de la préférence nationale la règle dans la commande publique et dans les cantines de l’Etat. Faso Mêbo et le Fonds de soutien patriotique l’ont déjà démontré : un peuple organisé peut financer et bâtir lui-même son avenir. Ce que nous avons fait pour nos routes et notre défense, nous pouvons le faire pour notre assiette, nos champs, nos usines et nos boutiques. Je demande donc à chacun de traduire ce patriotisme en actes simples, au quotidien : − au marché : demandons l’origine avant le prix. « D’où cela vient-il ? » doit précéder « combien cela coûte-t-il? » ; − dans le panier : choisissons le riz de nos plaines, notre huile, notre sucre, notre tomate, notre soumbala, nos céréales, plutôt que les produits venus d’ailleurs lorsque l’équivalent burkinabè existe ; − à la maison : servons au moins un repas entièrement burkinabè chaque jour. A nos invités, offrons le meilleur de notre cuisine, par fierté ; − aux cérémonies : baptêmes, mariages, funérailles, réceptions, privilégions les mets, les boissons et les tenues du pays. Le Faso Dan Fani et le kôkô dunda sont des tenues d’honneur ; − dans l’administration : cantines, pause-café, cadeaux protocolaires, fournitures et marchés publics doivent traduire la préférence nationale. C’est une obligation de service public. − à l’école : approvisionnons les cantines auprès des producteurs et des coopératives de la localité ; − au comptoir : commerçants et boutiquiers, mettez nos produits en première ligne de vos rayons et affichez clairement leur origine ; − à l’atelier et à l’usine : recherchons la qualité, soignons l’emballage, assurons la régularité et pratiquons le prix juste. Le patriotisme du consommateur exige en retour l’excellence du produit. − au champ et en brousse : produisons plus, produisons mieux, plantons et protégeons l’arbre. − jeunesse et diaspora : soyez les ambassadeurs du « Made in Burkina » partout où vous êtes. Chaque produit burkinabè que vous portez, offrez ou faites connaître ouvre un marché à un compatriote. Camarades, Notre souveraineté économique ne saurait se construire dans l’isolement. Elle prend tout son sens dans une Afrique qui produit, transforme et consomme davantage ce qu’elle crée elle-même. Le 29 juillet 1987, à Addis-Abeba, devant les chefs d’État africains, le camarade Thomas SANKARA lançait un appel qui n’a pas pris une ride, je le cite : « Faisons-en sorte également que le marché africain soit le marché des Africains : produire en Afrique, transformer en Afrique et consommer en Afrique. Produisons ce dont nous avons besoin et consommons ce que nous produisons au lieu de l’importer. » Trente-neuf ans après, cet appel demeure notre feuille de route. Avec nos frères de la Confédération des Etats du Sahel, ouvrons davantage nos marchés les uns aux autres : le lait de nos éleveurs, le riz de nos bas-fonds, le bétail de nos savanes et les tissus de nos métiers à tisser. Faisons du marché africain le marché des Africains. Au champ, produisons burkinabè ! À l’usine, transformons burkinabè ! Au marché, achetons burkinabè ! À table, consommons burkinabè ! La Patrie ou la Mort, nous Vaincrons ! Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ Président du Faso, Chef de l’État

items.title: Décès de Sidya Touré: dernières visites à un exilé jusqu’à la tombe!
items.description: L’ancien Premier ministre guinéen, Sidya Touré, décédé le samedi 26 septembre 2026 à Paris, dans sa 81e année, sera bel et bien inhumé en Côte d’Ivoire, loin de la terre de ses ancêtres, la Guinée. Wakat Séra avait été parmi les premiers médias à avoir annoncé cette information dans ses éditoriaux des 27 et 29 septembre. Certes, cette situation regrettable et déplorable à plus d’un titre, relevait de la volonté de sa famille d’enterrer le défunt à Abidjan, où il a longtemps été un serviteur de l’Etat très apprécié. Mais Abidjan est surtout une ville où il possédait une résidence qui pouvait accueillir ses obsèques, contrairement à Conakry en Guinée où, tout comme son compagnon de l’opposition, et également ancien Premier ministre, Cellou Dalein Diallo, il a été dépossédé de son domicile par les autorités militaires. C’est ainsi qu’à la suite de l’arrivée de la dépouille mortelle, le 2 octobre, en provenance de la capitale française, le domicile du président de l’Union des Forces républicaines (UFR), reçoit de nombreuses personnalités et des personnes anonymes qui y défilent pour saluer, la mémoire de «celui qui a vécu utile». Les hommages les plus poignantes se succèdent à la résidence mortuaire, sise aux quartier 2 Plateaux Vallon, depuis le dimanche 4, et ce, à ce mardi 6 octobre. De 16h à 20h, comme ce lundi 5 octobre, en présence d’une équipe de Wakat Séra, des délégations d’institutions, des anciens camarades de lycée et d’université, des parents, amis et proches de l’illustre disparu, en costumes, en boubous blancs ou en simple tenue de ville, ont effectué, dans un profond respect lié aux circonstances de deuil, l’une des dernières visites à Sidya Touré. En attendant la levée du corps et la prière mortuaire, prévues le jeudi 8 octobre, à la Grande mosquée de la Riviera Golf et l’inhumation qui, en principe, doit se dérouler, dans la foulée au cimetière de Williamsville, toujours à Abidjan, le recueillement se poursuit, rassemblant, en plus des proches de Sidya Touré vivant en Côte d’Ivoire, des amis, des proches et connaissances, des quatre coins du monde, d’anciens collaborateurs et des militants de partis politiques, venus de la Guinée ou d’ailleurs. Il en sera, sans doute, de même, lors des cérémonies du 3e, du 7e et du 40e jour, prévues à la Grande mosquée de la Riviera Golf, le dimanche 11 octobre. Les deux opposants guinéens en exil en Côte d'Ivoire, Sidya Touré (à gauche) et Cellou Dalein Diallo (Ph. d'archives) Au titre de ces partisans figurent en bonne place, les militants de l’Union des Forces démocratiques de Guinée (UFDG) qui ont sonné le tocsin de la mobilisation autour de leur leader, Cellou Dalein Diallo. Celui-ci se souvient de Sidya Touré, comme «d’un compagnon de toujours, d’un combattant de la liberté, d’un défenseur des droits humains et surtout d’un homme constamment en quête du mieux-être des Guinéens». Des valeurs qui collent également comme un gant, au président de l’UFDG contraint à l’exil en Côte d’Ivoire, depuis au moins cinq ans, comme son «frère Sidya». Non seulement les deux hommes ont été de toutes les luttes pour la défense de la Constitution, la libération du peuple guinéen du 3e mandat du Professeur Alpha Condé et la contestation du pouvoir de fer du général Mamady Doumbouya, mais ils sont aussi des compagnons d’exil en terre ivoirienne, ayant pour seul tort de s’être rangés aux côtés de Guinéens et de Guinéennes assoiffés de justice. Que fait donc la communauté internationale pour aider les Guinéens et Guinéennes dans leur quête constante d’un meilleur sort? Question à un plat de Konkoé, le savoureux poisson fumé guinéen! Que la terre ivoirienne soit légère à Sidya Touré et que sa mort en exil et son inhumation loin des siens et de ses ancêtres soient matière de réflexion pour les autorités guinéennes, afin qu’elles favorisent le retour à la maison, dans la paix et la justice, de tous les enfants du pays, pour la construction d’une Guinée où il fera bon vivre pour chacun et pour tous. Par Wakat Séra à Abidjan L’article Décès de Sidya Touré: dernières visites à un exilé jusqu’à la tombe! est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Octobre rose : « Le ministère de la Santé prévoit de dépister au moins 6 000 femmes », Pr Nayi Zongo
items.description: Chaque année, le monde entier dédie le mois d’octobre à la sensibilisation contre le cancer du sein. Ce mois dénommé : “octobre rose” est aussi commémoré au Burkina Faso où le gouvernement multiplie les efforts pour lutter contre la maladie. Dans cette interview, le coordonnateur du programme national de lutte contre le cancer, Pr Nayi Zongo, nous dépeint la situation de la maladie au niveau national et présente les grandes actions déjà menées ou en cours pour venir à bout du mal. Sidwaya (S) : Professeur, Expliquez-nous ce qu’est octobre rose ? N.Z. : Octobre rose est un mois consacré à la lutte contre le cancer du sein dans le monde. On a le ruban rose qui est devenu le symbole de la lutte contre le cancer et ce ruban a été popularisé surtout durant les mois d’octobre dans les années 1990. L’objectif d’octobre rose est d’obtenir un engagement des politiques, de plaider pour une mobilisation suffisante des ressources pour lutter efficacement contre le cancer du sein mais aussi de susciter une adhésion très forte des femmes au dépistage du cancers du sein. S : Quel est la situation du cancer du sein au niveau du Burkina ? N.Z. : Dans le monde, le cancer du sein est le cancer le plus fréquent. Au Burkina, il est le cancer le plus important et représente 20% de l’ensemble des cancers. Il est le cancer féminin responsable du plus grand nombre de décès suivi par le cancer du col de l’utérus. Selon les données de l’Observateur mondial sur le cancer, chaque jour qui passe, nous perdons trois femmes en ce qui concerne le cancer du sein et trois autres femmes pour le cancer du col de l’utérus au Burkina. S : Le ministère de la Santé a pris le lead dans la lutte contre ce cancer depuis un certain temps. Quel bilan peut-on faire aujourd’hui ? N.Z. : Cela fait trois ans que le ministère de la Santé commémore le mois d’octobre rose. Nous avons un bilan positif. D’abord, nous avons obtenu l’engagement des autorités politiques au plus haut niveau, ce qui fait que la lutte contre le cancer du sein de façon globale et particulièrement le cancer du sein est devenu une priorité parmi les priorités. Nous avons obtenu également l’engagement de la société civile, des partenaires techniques et financiers, des entreprises, des particuliers et du citoyen lambda. Quand vous regardez les réseaux sociaux, vous verrez de nombreux messages qui incitent les femmes à adhérer au dépistage du cancer du sein. Sur le plan des données chiffrées, concernant les deux commémorations d’octobre rose 2024 et 2025, nous avons pu dépister 230 000 lésions précancéreuses du col de l’utérus, 30 000 cancers du sein par écho mammographie. Nous avons également sensibilisé à travers le territoire national, près de 4 000 femmes qui sont maintenant bien outillées pour se protéger du cancer du sein et 2 millions de femmes ont appris à faire l’auto examen des seins. S : Pour cette année 2026, quels sont les objectifs que vous vous êtes fixés ? N.Z. : Cette année, le ministère de la Santé s’est fixé des objectifs ambitieux en phase avec la demande de la population. Pour octobre rose, le ministère prévoit, dépister par écho mammographie, au moins 6 000 femmes, dépister les lésions précancéreuses de l’utérus pour au moins 100 000 femmes et aussi sensibiliser au moins 2 millions de femmes sur le cancer du sein, sur le cancer du col de l’utérus. Il ambitionne également apprendre à près d’un million de femmes à s’examiner régulièrement les seins chaque mois. S : Disposez-vous des moyens pour réaliser toutes ses activités ? N.Z. : Il y a une implication très importante du gouvernement. Cet engagement se matérialise par les cliniques mobiles qui sont dans toutes les régions. Tout ce qui se fait à l’intérieur des cliniques mobiles rentre dans le cadre de la gratuité qui a été accordé par décret présidentiel. Ce qui fait que toutes les femmes ont accès maintenant aux dépistages. Pour atteindre ces chiffres, il nous faut communiquer et sensibiliser et nous comptons beaucoup sur les femmes et les médias pour accompagner le ministère de la santé dans ces tâches qui vont permettre de générer la demande afin que nous atteignions les objectifs cités. S : Quel mot avez-vous à l’endroit de la population à l’occasion de ce mois d’octobre rose ? N.Z. : J’ai d’abord un mot de remerciement aux autorités pour avoir fait de la lutte contre le cancer du sein une priorité, pour avoir permis que le dépistage par écho mammographie soit l’arme utilisée pour lutter contre le cancer du sein. Quand aux agents de santé, je leurs adresse surtout des remerciements pour leur dévouement, leur constance dans la lutte contre le cancer en général et le cancer du sein en particulier. Nous traduisons notre reconnaissance à nos associations de lutte contre le cancer et à nos partenaires techniques et financiers. Nous invitons la population à méditer sur le thème national d’octobre rose 2026 qui est : « Chaque dépistage est une vie sauvée et chaque vie de femme épargnée est une famille sauvegardée ». Pour qu’aucune femme ne meurt encore de cancer du col de l’utérus et du cancer de sein, mobilisons-nous. Interview réalisée par Samira Alida KAMBOU

items.title: Russia condemns Japan's sanctions package, vows countermeasures
items.description: Russia on Monday condemned Japan's 27th sanctions package as illegitimate and vowed to take proportionate countermeasures, focusing on areas of interest to Japan. "The Japanese government continues to take reckless steps that provoke further degradation of what little remains of that state's relations with Russia," Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said in a statement. On October 2, Tokyo announced its 27th package of measures against Russia, targeting 33 legal entities and nine individuals, as well as companies abroad. For the first time, the restrictions also cover shipping, Zakharova noted. Zakharova criticized Japanese authorities for attempting to justify the measures with the "current situation around Ukraine" and for presenting them as a "contribution to a peaceful settlement." "We see in this yet another confirmation of the lack of independence of the foreign policy course pursued by Tokyo, dictated not by national interests, but by Japan's reckless solidarity with the so-called like-minded countries in the Euro-Atlantic region," she said. (With input from Xinhua)

items.title: La Coalition pour l’éducation alerte sur les défis du corps enseignant
items.description: À l’occasion de la Journée mondiale des enseignants, célébrée chaque année le 5 octobre, la Coalition marocaine pour l’éducation pour tous appelle à une revalorisation profonde de la profession enseignante, qu’elle considère comme un levier indispensable à la garantie d’une éducation de qualité et inclusive. Dans un contexte international marqué par des tensions géopolitiques, des fragilités économiques et sociales, ainsi que par l’accélération des mutations technologiques et les effets croissants des changements climatiques, l’organisation estime que les systèmes éducatifs sont soumis à des pressions sans précédent. Au centre de ces transformations se trouvent les enseignants et les enseignantes, dont le rôle demeure, selon la Coalition, déterminant dans la formation des générations futures et dans la consolidation du capital humain nécessaire au développement. L’organisation considère que cette journée constitue une occasion de reconnaître leur contribution éducative et sociétale, mais aussi de mettre en lumière les difficultés professionnelles et matérielles qui affectent l’exercice de leur mission et limitent leurs capacités d’innovation. La Coalition s’appuie notamment sur les résultats de l’enquête internationale sur l’enseignement et l’apprentissage (TALIS 2024) réalisée au Maroc. Selon elle, cette étude met en évidence une faible autonomie pédagogique des enseignants, un niveau élevé de contraintes professionnelles et matérielles, ainsi qu’un sentiment d’insatisfaction à l’égard des rémunérations. Elle relève également que la charge de travail continue de peser sur la qualité des pratiques pédagogiques. Au-delà de ces constats, l’organisation estime que le corps enseignant demeure confronté à des obstacles structurels, notamment en matière de formation, de rémunération et de participation à l’élaboration des politiques éducatives et des programmes scolaires. Pour la Coalition, les droits des enseignants sont indissociables du droit à une éducation de qualité. Leur responsabilité dans l’accompagnement des enfants et des jeunes, leur rôle dans la socialisation et leur contribution à la protection des droits de l’enfance justifient, selon elle, une attention accrue des pouvoirs publics. L’organisation plaide ainsi pour une profession plus attractive, reposant sur des ressources humaines qualifiées bénéficiant de conditions salariales jugées équitables et respectueuses de la dignité professionnelle. Le communiqué appelle également à une refonte des curricula et des dispositifs de formation. La Coalition préconise un renforcement de la formation initiale et continue afin qu’elle soit adaptée aux mutations économiques, sociales, technologiques et environnementales. Elle considère que la formation doit constituer un droit tout au long de la carrière des enseignants et que ces derniers doivent être davantage associés à la définition des politiques éducatives et à l’évolution des programmes d’enseignement. L’organisation réclame par ailleurs une meilleure protection des droits sociaux des enseignants, notamment en matière de maternité et de paternité, ainsi que la mise en place de compensations adaptées pour les personnels exerçant dans les zones éloignées ou difficiles d’accès. Concernant l’enseignement privé, la Coalition appelle à un encadrement plus rigoureux du secteur. Elle demande la protection des droits professionnels et matériels des cadres éducatifs qui y travaillent, ainsi que la généralisation de contrats de travail clairs et équitables garantissant le respect de leur dignité. Elle plaide également pour un renforcement des mécanismes de contrôle afin d’assurer le respect des normes du travail décent au sein des établissements privés. Enfin, l’organisation insiste sur la nécessité de consolider les principes de transparence, de reddition des comptes et d’efficacité dans la gouvernance du système éducatif. Elle appelle à une implication effective des acteurs de l’éducation et de la société civile dans le suivi et l’évaluation des politiques publiques relatives à l’enseignement.
